entries.title: Chicago School Board approves budget that reverses layoffs, but counts on shaky state funds
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education made the unprecedented decision to reject the budget proposed by Chicago Public Schools’ superintendent Thursday and instead approved a revised plan that cancels more than 1,000 layoffs.</p><p>To do that, school board members are counting on the state to provide $150 million in state money that has yet to be committed — a move school district officials said was illegal and in violation of board members’ duties.</p><p>The board passed the amended budget 11-7. Board member Yesenia Lopez was the lone abstention. Board members who supported the amendment said that mass layoffs would be harmful to children and the warnings were overly severe. All the board members who voted in favor of changing the budget are aligned with the Chicago Teachers Union.</p><p>Meanwhile, board members Angel Gutierrez, Ellen Rosenfeld, Therese Boyle, Carlos Rivas, Che “Rhymefest” Smith, Jennifer Custer and Jessica Biggs voted no.</p><p>The vote came after a day of drama that included an unheard of two-hour recess. Board members said school district officials pressured them mid-meeting to abandon their plan to change the budget.</p><p>Emila Zoko, the district’s acting chief budget officer, issued stark warnings in her presentation to the board about the consequences of approving a budget that includes more money from the state than has yet to be appropriated.</p><p>She said the budget would not be seen as balanced, which is required under state law, and could result in a credit downgrade. That could, in turn, make it more expensive for the district to borrow money and pay off debt.</p><p>And, if state lawmakers don’t come through soon, the school district would have to cut spending midyear.</p><p>“If we count on this revenue and it fails to come through, it will be a disaster,” Zoko said.</p><p>Wally Stock, the acting chief financial officer, also said he is worried that if the district passes an unbalanced budget it may not be able to get the short-term loan needed to cover payroll in September. Supt. Macquline King echoed that concern and said it would be “catastrophic” not to get the loan, as staff who have not gotten paid all summer would continue to go without.</p><p>But board member Jitu Brown took issue with the warnings, calling them “fear mongering.” He looked at King and said he felt “disrespected and profoundly insulted” by the day’s conversations.</p><p>He said that there was political will now to increase funding for CPS. Illinois House and Senate leaders both said on Wednesday that they supported providing more state money to CPS, though there was no mention of specific figures<b>.</b></p><p>Board member Michilla Blaise put forth the amendment that reversed many of the district’s proposed cuts, saying that CPS leaders and her colleagues always talk about not making cuts to classrooms.</p><p>“These are real people in real schools,” she said. Blaise urged her colleagues not to “give the state a pass” because it “owes us money.”</p><p>And board member Debby Pope said she was “baffled” by the threats. The original budget proposed by district officials called for five furlough days and a spending freeze. All of these were to happen after January. If the state funding doesn’t come through, these drastic measures could be back on the table, she noted.</p><p>Much of the discussion centered on whether CPS should count on more state revenue, as the district is also counting on the city to pull funds from special taxing districts called TIFs. The city doesn’t decide how much money it can take out those TIFs until the fall, but King’s budget included $285 million from these special taxing districts.</p><p>King increased the TIF assumption on Monday and removed the possibility of furloughs after SEIU, which represents support staff, sent a letter demanding it.</p><p>Brown and others said it was hypocritical to do that with no real commitment from the city, and not to extend the same logic to the state.</p><p>Yet Board Member Che “Rhymefest” Smith and school district officials said they had good reason to believe that Mayor Brandon Johnson would come through with at least $285 million.</p><p>Before the vote, Supt. Macquline King publicly implored the board not to alter the budget so drastically. She reminded the board that 10 years ago the school district included shaky state revenue projections in the budget and wound up having to impose cuts in February.</p><p>At the time, she was a principal who had to tell staff they no longer had a job.<b> </b></p><p>“This was extremely disruptive to my students,” she said. “Those are the faces that I still see… We need to learn from our mistakes instead of repeating them.”</p><p>But board members also heard from a long line of teachers who told them how the layoffs of more than 1,600 staff would hurt students. They said they would rather keep school staff in place and fight for more state funding.</p><p>The vote marked the culmination of a tense budget process that kicked off with King’s announcement this spring that the school district faced a $732.5 million budget shortfall.</p><p>The deficit, which is about the same as last year’s, is the result of increasing costs to repair aging buildings, pay down debt and cover pensions and union contracts. The cost of special education has also shot up, as more students need services, while the state and federal government are falling short on their contributions.</p><p>CTU President Stacy Davis Gates backed the budget changes and urged board members to approve them. She noted that the budget already includes an assumption that Mayor Brandon Johnson will pull $285 million out of special taxing districts called TIFs, even though decisions about how much money could be available to taxing bodies like CPS are not made until the fall.</p><p>“You know what else is a safe assumption? That the governor follows the law and funds the schools,” Davis Gates said.</p><p>Everyone, from King to board members to union leaders, agreed that the long-term solution to CPS’ financial problems is more state funding. Time and again, speakers pointed to the 2017 state law that established how much school districts need to offer an adequate education to students.</p><p>Under that, CPS gets about 73% of what it needs from the state to provide an adequate education. To reach the adequacy bar, the state would have to increase CPS’ funding by about $1.6 billion a year, according to the state’s own formula.</p><p>Initially, state lawmakers set a goal of fully funding schools under the new formula by 2027. But at the rate the state is going, experts now say it will take another decade for that to happen.</p><p>King and several board members said it was too risky to assume that the state will come through with more money this year.</p><p>Dian Palmer, the president of SEIU Local 73, which represents CPS support staff, was not in favor of the board passing a budget that assumes the state will come through with more money because that could reopen the door to furloughs, she said.</p><p>Earlier this week, CPS removed five unpaid work days from the budget at the behest of staff unions who said the resulting pay cut was too deep.</p><p>“Waiting on Springfield is the risky path, and our children's education is not the place to take that risk,” Palmer said. “Every day this budget is delayed or built on a foundation that is not real money yet is a day of uncertainty for the workers that are trying to plan their lives and the families who are trying to plan their school year.”</p><p>Meanwhile, teachers spoke out at the board meeting about how staff cuts would affect their schools and urged the board to reverse teacher cuts.</p><p>Elizabeth Lundeen, a second grade teacher at DePriest Elementary School on the West Side, said her school lost several educators and was considering a drastic increase in class sizes.</p><p>“DePriest lost first, second, third and fourth grade teachers with no plans on how to fill these positions,” Lundeen said. The remaining fourth grade classroom would have 45 students, while the other grades would each have over 30 students, she added. “Not only are these class sizes untenable, the loss of these particular teachers is devastating.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago police searching for man who injured woman in hit-and-run crash on Lake Front trail
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are searching for a person who “catastrophically” injured a woman in a Gold Coast hit-and-run last week.</p><p>The woman was walking on the Lakefront trail near the 1400 N. Lake Shore Drive at 3:47 p.m. July 20 when she was hit by a man wearing a black ski mask and clothing, “recklessly” driving a yellow dirt bike, police said. She suffered "significant" injuries.</p><p>Anyone with information can contact detectives at (312) 745-4521.<br></p>

entries.title: Review: John Summit may be having the most fun at Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/07/30/photos-lorde-john-summit-headline-lollapalooza-day-1" >Lollapalooza 2026</a> will go down in history as the year when the pop girlies ruled the stage. And John Summit.</p><p>The Naperville born-and-bred DJ landed a slot at the same time as Lorde, one of five heavy-hitting women artists out of eight female headliners this year. For his headlining homecoming set, he pushed his usual high-energy performance past the max, riling up the crowd with “Chicago, let’s f- - - - - - go!” He opened with “Shadows” off his latest album, “Ctrl Escape,” turning the packed field in front of Bud Light stage into his personal club.</p><p>Summit posted to his Instagram stories earlier this week that Lollapalooza “inspired his crazy a-- journey in life.”</p><p>Just a few years ago he was working as an accountant and hustling as a DJ on the side, eventually saving enough to quit the stability of a corporate 9-to-5 job and taking a leap of faith to go off “the deep end” and all in on making music. At the time, the pandemic had shut everything down but Summit, born John Schuster, was just ramping up. </p><p>He submitted records to scores of labels, with one taking a chance. Defected Records released his track “Deep End,” which went viral and propelled his meteoric rise to global DJ stardom. He became known for his hypnotic, explosive tech house beats and infectious vocal hooks. He also built a following on social media, where he chronicles not just the headlining gigs on the festival circuit but also his day-to-day life like his workouts, embracing the cringe and making him accessible to millions of fans.</p><p>Summit’s Thursday Lollapalooza set was a rare headlining gig for a DJ. With his own independent label, Experts Only, and even his own EDM festivals (the second iteration of festival named after his label takes place in September in New York), as his collab track with Gorgon City goes, “The party's just begun. Is everybody having fun?” Perhaps no one is having more fun than John Summit. </p><p>Check out photos below from his headlining set Thursday night at the Bud Light Stage.</p><div entries.title: Man accused of shooting woman in Lincoln Park in June
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged with attempted murder in the shooting of a woman in Lincoln Park last month, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Jaylin Jones, 23, faces charges of attempted murder and aggravated battery, police said.</p><p>The 39-year-old woman was shot in the 600 block of West Belden Avenue on June 7, police said. She took herself to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she was in critical condition at the time.</p><p>Jones was slated to appear in court Thursday.</p>

entries.title: DiJonai Carrington jumps back in and helps the Sky finish
entries.summary: <p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> checked in during the second quarter to loud applause. Sky fans had waited long enough for that moment.</p><p>Carrington was one of the team's most exciting offseason additions — an athletic, defensive-minded wing who's also one of the league's most popular personalities. But she missed the first 27 games recovering from foot surgery.</p><p>She didn't want to rush back or pressure herself to play before she was ready. Even the day before the game, she wasn't sure she'd be able to play freely.</p><p>"I told myself the only way to figure it out is to jump in there and do it," she said.</p><p>The jump, after 10 months of rehab, went swimmingly. Carrington brought her signature defensive intensity in 17 minutes off the bench, getting a key block down the stretch to help seal the 94-88 victory over the Sun.</p><p>"It was really just instinct," Carrington said. "Once you're out there, I got a little groove and I stopped thinking and just started playing instinctively and I think that's the best way to play."</p><p>Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> said the Sky got exactly what they anticipated when they signed her: aggressive without forcing the issue on offense, tough and physical on defense. Even on a minutes restriction, Carrington played the entire fourth quarter, in which the Sky erased a five-point deficit, built a 12-point lead and — closing games being their Achilles heel all season — actually held it.</p><p>What was the difference this time?</p><p>"We were getting stops," Carrington said. "We were struggling to get stops late in games for the past couple months. And then two, we didn't stop going to what was working. We didn't overcomplicate it. What was working was [<b>Kamilla Cardoso</b>] in the middle of the floor. They didn't have no answer for it, so until they could stop it, we was gonna keep going to it. She made them pay every time."</p><p>The Sky initially defined themselves by their defense, particularly the ball pressure from their guards. That identity shifted as <b>Courtney Vandersloot</b> and <b>Azurá Stevens</b> got healthy and the offense took off — 94.4 points a game over the last 10.</p><p>Ideally, Carrington helps bridge both versions of the team.</p><p><b>Cardoso unplugs</b></p><p>The Sky kept going to the well with Cardoso in the fourth quarter. She all but clinched the game with 18 points in the frame, finishing with 26 and a season-high 11 free-throw attempts.</p><p>"The effort that she gave on both ends and the discipline that she showed on the defensive end in that…fourth quarter, it's commendable," Marsh said.</p><p>Clearly, a little rest agreed with her.</p><p>While All-Star Weekend festivities took over Chicago, Cardoso told the Sun-Times she was "in the house, just chilling."</p><p>She made a few appearances around the city, including a visit with her former Nike program, HER Elite. But she skipped the All-Star Game itself and didn't even tune in from home, fully unplugging for the weekend.</p><p><b>Stevens steps away</b></p><p>Stevens missed the Sun game for personal reasons after missing all three practices this week.</p><p>Rookie <b>Aicha Coulibaly</b> started in her place, though <b>Chloe Bibby</b> and <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> ended up sharing most of the minutes in the post.</p>

entries.title: One Wrigley Field memory still haunts Yankees skipper Aaron Boone
entries.summary: <p>After splitting four games with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox,</a> the Yankees will <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/30/new-york-yankees-week-in-chicago-aaron-boone-anthony-volpe-spencer-jones-cam-schlittler-michael-kay-cubs-white-sox-wrigley-field-rate-field" >remain in town</a> to take on the Cubs this weekend.</p><p>For manager Aaron Boone, the trip to Wrigley Field brings back one painful memory. It happened on what he said was “probably” his first visit.</p><p>Instead of a, um, friendly welcome, he got bonked in the head.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/30/new-york-yankees-week-in-chicago-aaron-boone-anthony-volpe-spencer-jones-cam-schlittler-michael-kay-cubs-white-sox-wrigley-field-rate-field" >Yankees making themselves at home during week in Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>As an 8-year-old in 1981, he and brother Bret got to accompany their dad Bob on a Philadelphia Phillies trip. The boys were playing in the outfield prior to a game at Wrigley when things took a painful turn for Aaron.</p><p>“It was a day game, obviously,” he said. “I was out in the outfield probably, literally 20, 30 minutes before the game. Bret’s hitting fly balls with the fungo. He hits one, I lose it in the sun, it hits me in the head. I’m down, out — literally out. The Phillies, some of the bullpen guys are starting to come out. They think I’m messing around. I wasn’t.”</p><p>Boone recalled Keith Moreland carrying him to the trainer’s room and being told not to fall asleep. Boone had a concussion.</p><p>“I lost one in the sun, was down for the count as an 8-year-old and recovering in the training room 10 minutes before gametime.”</p><h3>Walk it off</h3><h3></h3><p>The White Sox recorded their second walk-off win in as many days and ninth on the season on Thursday, when Tristan Thompson drew a bases-loaded walk in the 11<sup>th</sup> inning to give them a 2-1 victory.</p><p>It’s the first time they’ve done that since June 3-4, 2023, against Detroit, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.</p><h3>Stranding runners</h3><h3></h3><p>Though the White Sox rank among the majors’ leaders in scoring, they didn’t take advantage of their opportunities the past four games.</p><p>They were 9 for 37 with runners in scoring position and left 26 on base in the series. On Thursday, they were 2 for 9 and stranded 10.</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: White Sox again put in extra effort to beat Yankees
entries.summary: <p>Another impressive start by Sean Burke. Another tight victory over the New York Yankees. And a series split after dropping the first two games.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> will take it.</p><p>Tristan Peters drove in the winning run with a bases-loaded walk in the 11<sup>th</sup>, Sean Burke struck out 10 in six scoreless innings and the Sox beat the Yankees 2-1 on Thursday afternoon.</p><p>The AL Central-leading White Sox salvaged a split with another tight win after rallying to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/29/chicago-white-sox-new-york-yankees-12-innings-cam-schlittler-davis-martin-jordan-hicks-munetaka-murakami-sam-antonacci-ali-sanchez-ben-rice-will-venable-aaron-boone" >beat New York 6-5 in 12 innings on Wednesday night.</a> </p><p>“Going down two in a series is tough,” Peters said. “Taking it day by day is the only way we can do that. If we’re focused on those two losses, that just makes it build up and, like, snowball effect.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">BALL. 4. BALL. GAME. <a href="https://t.co/2Sbtx53pds">pic.twitter.com/2Sbtx53pds</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2082942416462434799?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Burke kept his string of dominant outings going on a day when New York starter Ryan Weathers was every bit as good. He held the White Sox to three hits in seven innings.</p><p>Sox lefty Chris Murphy gave up an RBI single to New York’s Trent Grisham in the 10<sup>th</sup> that made it 1-0. The White Sox tied it in the bottom half on Andrew Benintendi’s pinch-hit single against Angel Chivilli.</p><p>Seranthony Domínguez got out of a second-and-third jam in the top of the 11<sup>th</sup> when Anthony Volpe grounded out.</p><p>The White Sox loaded the bases with one out in the bottom half of the 11th against Fernando Cruz on an infield single by Sam Antonacci.</p><p>Colson Montgomery went ahead 3-0 in the count before striking out. Peters then walked on four pitches to bring in the winning run and set off the celebration. He ran into the outfield before teammates caught up to him and pulled off his jersey.</p><p>“You lose the first two of four, it’s like, alright, let’s just scrap and maybe (win) at least one,” Benintendi said. “Especially against a team like that, the arms they have, it shows a lot about what we have in here.”</p><p>Burke continued his string of dominant performances, giving up just three hits and walking two while finishing one strikeout shy of his season and career high. The 6-6 right-hander has a 1.42 ERA over his past eight appearances, a stretch that started with a dominant performance in a win at Yankee Stadium on June 18.</p><p>“Today, I threw a couple changeups and I was able to get strikes on them and bad swings on them,” Burke said. “That’s something I think I’m gonna lean on a little bit more as time goes on, just mixing that in when some of the other stuff is not as sharp. I just feel good with all that stuff now. The game plans coming in have been good.”</p><p>Sean Newcomb worked two scoreless innings, and Bryan Hudson retired all three batters in the ninth.</p><p><sup></sup></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>“Tough couple games,” manager Will Venable said. “We really had to grind it. Contributions from everybody. Obviously, extra innings, there’s a ton of situational stuff that you have to execute, and guys really executed well.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Review: Sombr, with margarita in hand, struts into Lollapalooza like he owns the place
entries.summary: <p>Some may still question Sombr’s overnight rockstar status, but he certainly doesn’t. The 21-year-old entered Lollapalooza Thursday like he owned the place, getting an escort to the stage in a classic muscle car and stepping out in a blaze, complete with feather boa, sunglasses, cigarette in mouth and margarita in hand.</p><p>The only other person who might be able to pull off that kind of bravado this weekend is Billy Corgan, whom Sombr has gleaned inspiration from in the past. While the Smashing Pumpkins frontman didn’t make an appearance with the young star (born Shane Michael Boose) like he did previously at April’s Coachella, other special guests did, including 5 Seconds Of Summer, who Sombr hailed as “the greatest band in the f—-ing world.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The stage was designed to look like an urban construction zone, hinting at a “work in progress” theme that has become a big part of the young artist’s appeal.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The pop rock band ran through their own song “She Looks so Perfect” while Sombr basically milled about. It was an unnecessary touch and an odd pairing for Sombr’s ‘70s glam rock style. It’s not like the rising talent needed the extra lift anyway. He already drew the biggest crowd of the weekend up to this point with bodies stretching from the T-Mobile Stage back to the break at Balbo Street to hear signature hits “Undressed,” “12 to 12,” new song “Potential” and a few lines of Djo’s Chicago theme song “End of Beginning.”</p><p>Sombr is not the Lou Reed-Marc Bolan-Bowie messiah for the new millennium that some would claim him to be, but song is about my issues with body image, a struggle I’ve had my whole life,” he shared while introducing new song “My Body Isn’t Ready.” (In another recent baller move, he got “Obsession” star Inde entries.title: Trump administration stops work on Great Lakes Asian carp project near Joliet
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker is calling on the Trump administration to immediately reverse a work stoppage on an embattled project needed to keep invasive Asian carp out of the Great Lakes near Joliet.</p><p>Contractors at the Brandon Road Interbasin Project received a work stoppage order on July 24 stating the project is under administrative review, despite about $2 million worth of material already on site. Work was slated to begin this week, with shaft drilling scheduled for September. Jobsite trailers were also already set up at the project, according to Will County officials.</p><p>"Under my administration, Illinois has spearheaded this project to protect the entire Great Lakes region. Yet, the Trump Administration repeatedly throws up roadblocks and has now ordered work to stop altogether with no explanations,” Pritzker said Thursday<b>.</b> “The Great Lakes provide drinking water to more than 40 million people and support a $52 billion regional economy. It's time for the Trump Administration to uphold the federal government’s obligations, stop playing political games, and move this project forward.”</p><p>The $1.15 billion project in the Des Plaines River near Joliet is seen as a crucial way to stop invasive Asian carp from entering the Great Lakes. Without a barrier, the carp could wreak havoc on the $20 billion fishing and boating industries and upend the freshwater ecosystem, experts say. The species already has made it into the Illinois River from the Mississippi River. Fishermen contracted by the state of Illinois have removed more than 78 million pounds of invasive carp from waterways.</p><p>There have been several delays to the project, including a pause in December for another administrative review. President Donald Trump in March said "only Trump" could save the Great Lakes from Asian carp and urged governors to "join in on the fight." Those words on social media came after he met with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, prompting both Pritzker and Sen. Dick Durbin to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/13/jb-pritzker-dick-durbin-invasive-asian-carp-wants-great-lakes-donald-trump-brandon-road-interbasin-project" target="_blank" >demand Trump lift the review and release federal funds</a> on the Joliet project.</p><p>The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in April instead <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/04/10/great-lakes-brandon-road-carp-to-michigan" target="_blank" >announced that it would put Michigan officials in charge of the $1.15 billion barrier</a> designed to keep the invasive carp from reaching the Great Lakes — moving from the Rock Island district to its Detroit District.</p><p>Both sides engaged in a war of words in April, with Pritzker calling the move a “political stunt” and warning that Illinois would explore legal action if the Trump administration broke legally-binding agreements. In announcing the move, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Adam Telle accused Illinois of being an “unreliable partner, delinquent on its payments and real estate commitments,” a claim that Pritzker denied. </p><p>The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said it first learned of the work stoppage through contractors — and followed through on a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on Thursday, with the work stoppage confirmed on July 28 after repeated attempts to reach their Detroit District.</p><p>Renee Snow, interim IDNR director, wrote in a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers that she wants an “immediate” meeting to “substantiate the work stoppage and remedy project cost, schedule, and partnership impacts.”</p><p>Snow wrote that the breakdown in communication is inconsistent with procedures established under a jointly negotiated plan that guided the project. </p><p>Gary G. Perinar III, president of Carpenters Local 174 in Joliet, told the Sun-Times the project delays “not only endanger the safety of the Great Lakes but also negatively affect the working men and women who have supported this project locally.”</p><p>“This project needs to happen,” Perinar III said. “...Our members stand by eagerly awaiting the opportunity to get the job done building and strengthening our communities.”</p><p>The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday. <br></p>

entries.title: Northwestern coach David Braun professes championship mentality for Wildcats
entries.summary: <p>David Braun may or may not have a starting quarterback yet.</p><p>The Northwestern coach wasn't ready to talk about that Thursday as Big Ten Media Days wrapped up at the Hilton Chicago. But he had plenty to say about where the bar should be set for a program that won its last Big Ten title in 2000.</p><p>After paying tribute to the heavy lifting done by previous coaches Gary Barnett, Randy Walker and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/07/29/michigan-state-pat-fitzgerald-northwestern-big-ten-media-days" >Pat Fitzgerald,</a> Braun said the Wildcats "have expectations to do it better than we've ever done it before.</p><p>"Big Ten championship, why not us?</p><p>"Host a College Football Playoff game at new Ryan Field, why not us?</p><p>"Aspire to chase down a national championship, why not us?"</p><p>A cynic might point to Northwestern's football history. The Wildcats have never won more than 10 games in a season, and they've only done that five times. They've never been higher than seventh in the final Associated Press rankings. Most programs have peaks and valleys over the years, but for Northwestern it's been more hills and canyons.</p><p>Still, there's no doubt the Wildcats are no longer the Big Ten also-rans they were in the decades before Barnett arrived in 1992. There were notable highlights under Fitzgerald, including 10-win seasons in 2015 and 2017. And Braun did well just to hold the program together when he took over in 2023 in the wake of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/northwestern-hazing-scandal" >hazing scandal.</a></p><p>Still, a Big Ten championship, a home playoff game, contending for a national title?</p><p>Braun said the pieces are in place for a golden age of Northwestern football. He touted the leadership of new president Mung Chiang, athletic director Mark Jackson and megadonor Pat Ryan Jr., the driving force behind the Wildcats' new stadium that will open in October.</p><p>Another bullet point: Northwestern returns 88% of the eligible returning snaps from last year's 6-6 team — something of a rarity in the portal age. That includes leading rusher Caleb Komolafe and the top two receivers: Griffin Wilde and Hayden Eligon II.</p><p>But who will hand off to Komolafe and throw to the receivers?</p><p>Preston Stone, last year's starter, is gone, but there are a couple of transfers who were Power Four QB1s elsewhere. Aidan Chiles lost his starting job at Michigan State two-thirds of the way through a 4-8 season, while Nicco Marchiol was West Virginia's starter until a foot injury ended his 2025 season in Week 4. Ryan Boe, who saw limited action as last year's backup, returns.</p><p>"We're not in a position right now to name a starter," Braun said. "But we won't be going into Week 1 worrying about our quarterback."</p><p>Be that as it may, all signs point to Chiles being the guy. "He's a freak athlete — 6-5, long, has a cannon," Wildcats safety Robert Fitzgerald said. "He is very fast. So I'm very excited to see what him and the offense and Chip Kelly can do. I think they're going to be very explosive."</p><p>The hope is that Kelly — "arguably the best offensive coordinator in all of college football history," according to Braun — can elevate an offense that has often been the team's Achilles' heel in recent seasons.</p><p>Then, who knows?</p><p>"I feel like we're always overlooked," Komolafe said. "Our mentality shouldn't be just to get to a bowl game or six wins or this or that. Honestly, we should be a 12-0 team that wants to go to the Big Ten championship and then ultimately play in the College Football Playoff."</p><p>That's what his coach likes to hear.</p>

entries.title: ChiArts funding vote postponed as CPS board debates budget consequences
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education has postponed a vote that would have provided extra funding for the school formerly known as the Chicago High School for the Arts — putting its vaunted professional arts training program in limbo a few weeks before the start of the school year.</p><p>The resolution was meant to be the culmination of months of advocacy by the ChiArts community after the leaders of the privately run but publicly funded school voted against renewing their contract with Chicago Public Schools because of financial deficits.</p><p>Amid fears the school would shutter, CPS stepped in and absorbed it as a fine and performing arts school recently renamed Chicago Arts High School. But parents, students and teachers argued that keeping the doors open wasn’t enough.</p><p>They wanted CPS to maintain its current flagship arts training program, as well as retain the teaching artists responsible for executing it — otherwise, they said layoffs and school schedule changes risked upending the fabric of the school that has produced a bevy of professional artists, including talents such as R&B <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/07/30/ravyn-lenae-chicago-high-school-arts-lollapalooza-sabrina-carpenter" target="_blank" ><u>singer Ravyn Lenae</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-570000" name="image-570000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>ChiArts music conservatory teaching artist Kyle Cortés spoke at a rally in May protesting the loss of many artists-in-residence at the school. Cortés was among the teaching artists told their contract would not be renewed.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Board of Education member Michilla Blaise of the West Side introduced a resolution this month calling on the district to provide one year of extra funding so the school can retain its current arts programming and staff in the upcoming school year — $5.5 million according to previous district estimates.</p><p>That would give the school time to figure out a plan to raise the money on its own in subsequent years, Blaise said, adding that she wanted to support a “gem” in the district’s portfolio even though the school isn’t in her district — it is in board member Carlos Rivas’ area.</p><p>“I really do think that ChiArts will be in a position where it can raise its own money and it will be able to earn its own keep,” Blaise said at Thursday’s meeting. “The imperative part of this is because the teaching artists have been laid off.”</p><p>But after a heated debate over the school district’s $732 million budget deficit, some board members challenged the plan to give more money to one school when many others are also in need of resources. Questions also remained about where exactly the money would come from.</p><p>As a result, Blaise decided to table the resolution until late August, after the start of the school year. The board unanimously approved.</p><p>CPS officials had said there would be challenges maintaining ChiArts’ programming, including the requirement that art classes at district-run schools must be taught by a certified teacher — and many of the professional teaching artists at the school don’t have that certification.</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for the district said CPS is committed to preserving the conservatory model but the resolution would force the district to review school budgets and could lead to cuts at other schools.</p><p>“Allocating an extra $5 million to a single school would give it nearly 100 times more support than its counterparts, creating severe systemic inequality,” the statement said. “CPS remains committed to supporting our students, families, and staff at Chicago Arts High School while upholding our fiduciary responsibility to treat all 73 fine arts schools across Chicago equitably.”</p><p>Given the district’s financial constraints, Grammy Award-winning school board member Che “Rhymefest” Smith said at Thursday’s board meeting that he worried the extra money would be taken from other schools.</p><p>“What we are effectively doing is we’re saying we’ll take from arts for the whole city just for one school,” Smith said.</p><h3>Big changes expected</h3><p>The school day at ChiArts ran from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Five hours were dedicated to academics, and the conservatory portion ran uninterrupted for three hours in the afternoon. Similar to a charter school, the academic day was funded by public dollars and the three-hour conservatory arts training was supported by donors through a foundation.</p><p>Students who have spoken at board meetings over the past few months said they wanted the school to remain as is, crediting the conservatory program for helping them grow as artists and people.</p><p>“I don't want my senior year experience to be reduced to a singular generalized art class due to the reduction of our staff,” rising senior Shaelan Wallace said. “I want the students who come after me to be able to experience the same rich exposure to the arts that I have had.”</p><p>But the district says it has to make changes, such as shortening the school day, due to labor agreements and other factors including its own financial woes.</p><p>Incoming Principal Casey Fuess revealed earlier this year that the school day is being shortened by 50 minutes and will run from 8:10 a.m. to 4:20 p.m. School leaders said the old nine-hour school day was the longest of any major public arts high school in the country, and the new length is still longer than the majority of comparable schools.</p><p>That means students will have 150 minutes of arts instruction instead of 180 in the old conservatory model, but school leaders say after-school programming will help make up for that lost time.</p><p>Arts instruction will no longer be reserved for the end of the day — those minutes will be mixed into a student’s regular school day schedule. Some students raised concerns that breaking up the conservatory's consecutive hours of arts instruction could be harmful for some disciplines — such as writing and music — where students need extra time to be creative and practice.</p><p>Other changes include layoffs of ChiArts staff. Megan Pietz, chair of the Chicago Teachers Union council at ChiArts, said 13 academic teachers would not return next year.</p><p>The district also plans to reduce the number of teaching artists from last year’s 70 and could create 20 part-time district-wide “resident artist” positions that could be deployed to the school.</p><p>In a message to the community, Fuess explained that as a contract school ChiArts operated under an exemption that allowed charter and contract schools to use teachers who are not licensed by the state to teach credit-bearing courses. But as a CPS-managed school, teachers must be licensed in order for students to earn credits and meet graduation requirements.</p><p>“This requirement has significant implications for staffing at the school, and has led to some of the difficult staffing decisions we have had to make,” Fuess wrote.</p><p>Filip Lewandowski, an English teacher at ChiArts, said he recognized the district’s tough financial situation but asked the board to give the school time to find funds to maintain its culture.</p><p>“It preserves the conservatory while ChiArts stakeholders establish the partnerships and financial supports needed to sustain it,” Lewandowski said Thursday. “ChiArts will bring in more revenue if CPS invests in its preservation."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/25/cps-eyes-changes-to-chiarts-conservatory-model-upsetting-parents-who-want-more-arts-during-school-day" >CPS eyes changes to ChiArts conservatory model, upsetting parents who want more arts during school day</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/10/09/cps-proposes-taking-over-chiarts-but-allowing-a-small-charter-school-to-close" >CPS proposes taking over ChiArts, but allowing a small charter school to close</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Project Exploration students know what they did this summer
entries.summary: <p>William Slaughter has spent more than four years mentoring other young people through Project Exploration, an educational nonprofit that, among other things, helps students explore career possibilities through its summer programs.</p><p>Positive community programs like that have a real impact, Slaughter believes, and on Thursday at Columbus Park, that impact was on display.</p><p>During a showcase at the Columbus Park Refectory, students got to show off what they'd been doing this summer.</p><p>Some got a taste of a range of career interests. Others worked on projects in the fields of science, technology, engineering and mathematics.</p><p>"If you give us other places to have fun that encourage positivity, structure, and discipline, we’ll be good. We’ll be powerful," said Slaughter, who just graduated from Illinois State University.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-540000" name="image-540000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f04638b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5476x3073+0+289/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F64%2Fe7%2Fbb2f1cf14404ad16ac0113605f45%2Fprojectexploration-260731-04.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87882be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5476x3073+0+289/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F64%2Fe7%2Fbb2f1cf14404ad16ac0113605f45%2Fprojectexploration-260731-04.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/97bc2f9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5476x3073+0+289/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F64%2Fe7%2Fbb2f1cf14404ad16ac0113605f45%2Fprojectexploration-260731-04.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="William Slaughter, 22, checks on a brood of chicks at the Columbus Park Refectory in Austin on Thursday July 30, 2026. entries.title: What to know after tornadoes tore through Chicago suburbs
entries.summary: <p>Powerful storms that swept across the Chicago area Monday left neighborhoods in the south suburbs picking up the pieces after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" >seven tornadoes touched down</a> — damaging homes, uprooting trees and adding to what has already been an active tornado season in Illinois.</p><p>An EF1 tornado with peak winds of 110 mph impacted Lansing, according to the National Weather Service. The fifth tornado, an EF0 that touched down just south of Wheaton College, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/29/5th-tornado-confirmed-monday-storms-national-weather-service" >was confirmed Wednesday</a>.</p><p>Rob Griffin, a Lansing resident, told the Chicago Sun-Times he underestimated the severity of the storm that hit his far south suburb.</p><p>"Even though they had the sirens on and sent alerts to our phones, I kind of ignored it because most times they do that as more of a warning," Griffin said. "So I didn’t heed the warning.”</p><p>As tornado season continues to surge across Illinois, here's what you need to know.</p><h3><b>What happened during Monday’s storms?</b></h3><p>Five powerful storms swept across the Chicago area Monday, according to the National Weather Service, causing significant damage to homes and trees. They also brought significant rainfall, with McCook Reservoir nearing capacity. It was just the latest episode in what already has been an active tornado season in Illinois.</p><p>For Lansing resident Abo Lorebelo, the storm was unlike anything he had experienced in the four years he's lived there. He and his family sheltered in their basement while the tornado moved through, but their home suffered major roof damage.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Why are there so many tornadoes in Illinois this year?</b></h3><p>So far this year, Illinois has experienced a record number of tornadoes.</p><p>Meteorologists say multiple rounds of severe weather this spring and summer have contributed to the elevated tornado count.</p><p>Before Monday's storms, the weather service estimated the state already had recorded 183 tornadoes, far surpassing the previous record of 142 tornadoes, set in 2024. The total is expected to change as the weather service routinely updates its storm survey database.</p><h3><b>Can tornadoes happen in the Chicago area?</b></h3><p>Yes, and they have.</p><p>While many people associate tornadoes with rural communities, Monday’s storms served as another reminder that tornadoes can affect communities throughout Chicago and its suburbs.</p><p>Victor Gensini, director of Northern Illinois University’s Center for Interdisciplinary Research on Convective Storms, has previously warned residents never to assume tornadoes cannot hit densely populated areas.</p><h3><b>What should I do after a tornado alert?</b></h3><p>Illinois state climatologist Trent Ford said every Midwesterner should have the proper plans in place in the event of severe weather warnings, making sure family members are safe and together and know what to do. Things like going down into the basement (if you have one) and keeping your phone and other electronic items charged in case of outages. Also make sure to follow messaging from the National Weather Service.</p><p>Some residents admitted they, like Griffin in Lansing, underestimated Monday's storm despite emergency alerts being sent to cellphones and the blaring of tornado sirens.</p><p>"I think they're doing a good job of warning us," said Griffin, who lost nearly all of his roof during the storm. "Hopefully, we, as citizens, will take heed to that."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5d0000" name="image-5d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/02bfd0b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fab%2F025e9fd34eaf85c3660a5370a5c6%2Ftornadoexplainer-260730-015-griffin.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8127b35/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fab%2F025e9fd34eaf85c3660a5370a5c6%2Ftornadoexplainer-260730-015-griffin.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1d57dae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2Fab%2F025e9fd34eaf85c3660a5370a5c6%2Ftornadoexplainer-260730-015-griffin.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rob Griffin outside his storm-damaged home near 192nd Place and Oakwood Avenue in Lansing on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Griffin’s immediate priority is covering the exposed structure after nearly the entire roof was ripped off Monday, the day a tornado hit the city.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Are tornadoes becoming more common in Illinois?</b></h3><p>To see just how active the 2026 tornado season has been, consider this.</p><p>The University of Illinois climatologist's office added up how many tornadoes occurred in the state in July over the 70-year span from 1950-2020. The answer: 181.</p><p>That's 181, total. Over all 70 years.</p><p>With the 2026 statewide tally, Illinois already has exceeded that total in less than a year. </p><p>So while tornado activity can change from year to year, 2026's activity has reached the highest point in recent years.</p><p>Still, it doesn't mean Illinois is the new Tornado Alley. Yet.</p><p>That phrase is a “media colloquialism” coined in the early 1950s and is in no way an official designation, Gensini has previously cautioned the Sun-Times.</p><p>“If I ask 100 of my meteorology friends to define" what Tornado Alley is, he said, "they’d each have a different answer."</p><p>According to some definitions, Illinois actually has been considered part of Tornado Alley for some time. Initially, the nickname applied to Southwestern states ravaged by twisters in the last century, such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.</p><h3><b>Is climate change causing more tornadoes?</b></h3><p>The answer isn't straightforward.</p><p>Ford told the Sun-Times warmer temperatures and increased moisture in the atmosphere can create environments that favor stronger thunderstorms.</p><p>However, researchers say the relationship between climate change and tornadoes themselves remains less certain.</p><p>Ford said a warmer, more humid climate may be contributing to more environments favorable for severe storms, though scientists are still studying exactly how those conditions affect tornado frequency.</p><h3><b>What happens next?</b></h3><p>The National Weather Service will continue surveying storm damage across the region throughout the week to determine the final strength and paths of Monday’s tornadoes.</p><p>As cleanup continues, many Lansing residents say the storm has changed how they will respond the next time severe weather warnings are issued. For Griffin and others across the south suburbs, Monday’s storms were a reminder that preparation and taking warnings seriously can make a difference when severe weather entries.title: Jaguars coach bemoans attention given Bears QB Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>Jaguars coach Liam Coen thinks his team is overlooked — and that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/30/bears-training-camp-report-practice-no-2" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> is not.</p><p>Thursday, he invoked the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback when telling 1010 XL-AM in Jacksonville how he was thankful that the Jaguars were perennially under the radar. He said he preaches to his staff that “the best part of coaching” the Jaguars is his players knowing they’re not part of the national conversation.</p><p>Along the way, the Bears quarterback caught a stray. Williams noticed, too. On X, he reposted the video of Coen’s comment.</p><p><i>“</i>You don’t have to make up the fire,” Coen said. “You don’t have to make it up. It’s given to us every day. It’s a gift from the heavens. I just go pull out of my phone, look up the NFL Network web site and just pop it up here and I’m curious if I see any photos, or anything, about the Jacksonville Jaguars. I think I’ll just scroll right on through. </p><p>"I think I’ll see 40 pictures of Caleb Williams and I won’t see a single thing about any of players on here. So it’s beautiful … I’m going to tell these guys how much you all think they suck, and we’ll keep going.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">“All I’ll see is 40 pictures of Caleb Williams… and not a single thing about any of our players.” 😂<br><br>Liam Coen had a hilarious way of describing why he loves coaching the Jaguars on The Drill with Dan Hicken and Jeff Prosser.<br><br>🎥 WATCH NOW: <a href="https://t.co/E5etiiSE3n">https://t.co/E5etiiSE3n</a><a href="https://x.com/hashtag/DUUUVAL?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#DUUUVAL</a> |… <a href="https://t.co/idQZCvDMkK">pic.twitter.com/idQZCvDMkK</a></p>— 1010 XL / 92.5 FM (@1010XL) <a href="https://x.com/1010XL/status/2082949597261910044?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams, who is on the cover of this year’s “Madden” video game, was named the No. 51 player in the NFL Top 100 last week. Trevor Lawrence, Coen's quarterback, was No. 62.<br></p>

entries.title: Contractor who died in Downers Grove storm sewer identified
entries.summary: <p>A contractor who died after becoming trapped in a Downers Grove storm sewer during heavy rain Monday has been identified as 33-year-old Ivan A. Perez, of Pasadena, Texas, the DuPage County coroner's office confirmed late Thursday.</p><p>Perez's body was recovered Tuesday in the 5100 block of Washington Street, according to DuPage County Coroner Judith Lukas.</p><p>The probable cause of death was accidental drowning, pending toxicology results, the coroner's office said.</p><p>“Our office would like to express our deepest condolences to Ivan Perez's family, friends, and coworkers,” Lukas said in a statement.</p><p>Perez was one of two contractors who became trapped Monday while working on a pipe rehabilitation project after storms moved through the area.</p><p>The other worker was rescued about 200 feet down the sewer and taken to Advocate Good Samaritan Hospital in Downers Grove in good condition.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.suntimeswire.com/news/2026/07/28/downers-grove-sewer-storm-drain" target="_blank" ><u>Occupational Safety and Health Administration is investigating</u></a> the incident.</p>

entries.title: Sun-Times reporter's Lithuania ties resonate
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/07/22/stephanie-zimmermann-why-lithuania-chicago-longworth-media-fellowship" >“Why Lithuania?”</a> Stephanie Zimmermann's editor asked her. I’ve been on the receiving end of that question for the last 10 years. My body could feel the jolt she described feeling when a roadside sign matched a name in her grandparents' memoir; it was replaying my second trip to Lithuania when I visited Anykščiai for the first time.</p><p>I have chased that same thread across Lithuania more times than I can count. In 2016, I joined a company founded by Lithuanian immigrants in Chicago, unaware of my own family connection to the country. That summer, before my first trip, my uncle Steven Kowalsky handed me a handwritten letter from his father, Larry, born Khona Leyzys Kovalskis, which told his immigration story from Lithuania to the United States.</p><p>Larry was born in Anykščiai, the son and grandson of the town blacksmith. The family lived on a wooden-house street later renamed for the aviators Steponas Darius and Stasys Girėnas, just over 60 miles from the capital city of Vilnius.</p><p>In 2017, on my second trip, my Lithuanian co-workers drove me to Anykščiai. Using a letter from my great uncle Larry as my map, I found the exact corner where his mother once kept her grocery store. I stood where, as a boy, he had run to the river and the great boulder called Puntukas.</p><p>Larry, his mother and most of his siblings reached America. His father and one sister did not and were killed after the Germans came.</p><p>Larry's memoir was published in Lithuania in a collection titled "Gyvieji tiltai" — Living Bridges. Both Larry and Steven have passed away, but I know they would both be happy and proud that Lithuania has become such a significant part of my own story. In 2024, I joined the founding team at <a class="Link" href="https://gritmind.com/about-us/" target="_blank" >Gritmind</a>, where I am a partner and head of artificial intelligence products. We are co-headquartered in Kaunas, Vilnius and Chicago. In my own way I’m continuing to bridge our family’s past and present.</p><p>Next summer, I hope to bring my own family to that corner in Anykščiai, so the bridge reaches one more generation.</p><p><i>Laura Graves, Jefferson Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>More Stars coverage, please </h3><p>It's wonderful to see the close attention the Sun-Times pays to the Chicago Sky. Nevertheless, the Sky aren't the only women’s game in town. The National Women's Soccer League has a team here: the Chicago Stars. The Sun-Times' coverage of this team is virtually nonexistent. This failure exists despite the presence of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/stars/2026/05/27/mallory-swanson-uswnt-triple-espresso-stars-fire-gm-richard-feuz" >Mallory Swanson</a>, an internationally known athlete in Chicago sports. Shame!</p><p><i>Bert Rice, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Brush up on ‘The Odyssey’ before watching film</h3><p>If you're thinking about seeing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/06/10/christopher-nolan-odyssey-adaptation-film-homer-joe-goodkin" >“The Odyssey,”</a> get CliffsNotes first. Watching the almost three-hour epic with my wife showed how little one really learns through the embellished movies over the years. Maybe Homer and other classics should be back on the required reading lists.</p><p><i>Walt Gorman, Bridgeport</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: Trump's new tariffs are just as questionable as his previous ones
entries.summary: <p>When you start with a predetermined policy and then go looking for a legal pretext to justify it, you are building on shaky ground. President Donald Trump illustrated that point once again last week, when he <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/07/actions-by-the-united-states-in-the-investigations-under-section-301-of-the-trade-act-of-1974-of-the-acts-policies-and-practices-of-60-economies-related-to-the-failure-of-each-economy-to-impose-and/" target="_blank" >announced</a> a third round of broad tariffs after his first two attempts were rejected by federal courts.</p><p>Shortly after taking office last year, Trump claimed to have discovered a previously unnoticed delegation of tariff authority in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/50/chapter-35" target="_blank" >International Emergency Economic Powers Act</a>, a 1977 law that does not mention import taxes and had never been used to impose them. Under the act, Trump argued, he could tax imports of any goods he decided to target from any country he chose at any rate he deemed appropriate for any length of time he thought was necessary.</p><p>Trump's claim was rejected by every court that considered it, including the Supreme Court, which last February <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/02/20/the-supreme-court-just-struck-down-trumps-emergency-tariffs/" target="_blank" >ruled</a> that the act does not authorize tariffs at all. But Trump had a backup plan: Immediately after that decision, he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/02/20/trump-orders-new-10-percent-global-tariff-after-supreme-courts-rebuke/" target="_blank" >announced</a> another sweeping set of tariffs, this time relying on Section 122 of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/COMPS-10384/pdf/COMPS-10384.pdf" target="_blank" >Trade Act of 1974</a>.</p><p>That provision allows tariffs in response to "fundamental international payments problems" caused by "serious United States balance-of-payments deficits." In May, the U.S. Court of International Trade <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/07/federal-court-trumps-newest-tariffs-are-also-illegal/" target="_blank" >ruled</a> that the new tariffs were illegal because Trump had failed to "identify balance-of-payments deficits within the meaning of Section 122."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Although that decision was <a class="Link" href="https://www.troutman.com/insights/federal-circuit-hits-pause-on-cits-section-122-tariff-ruling/" target="_blank" >stayed</a> pending appeal, Trump's Section 122 tariffs, which were subject to a 150-day statutory limit, expired July 24. Trump then <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/24/trumps-newest-tariffs-are-likely-illegal-too/" target="_blank" >switched</a> to Plan C, invoking Section 301 of the Trade Act, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2411" target="_blank" >authorizes</a> tariffs in response to a foreign "act, policy, or practice" that is "unreasonable or discriminatory" and "burdens or restricts United States commerce."</p><p>The latest tariffs <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-takes-action-forced-labor-section-301-investigations" target="_blank" >supposedly target</a> countries that have failed to "impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor." Because of that failure, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Press/Releases/2026/FLIP%20301%20Investigation%20Final%20Action%20FRN%207-23-26%20FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" >says</a>, U.S. businesses face unfair and unethical competition from foreigners who use forced labor to keep their costs and prices low.</p><p>The list of alleged offenders is long. Greer <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-takes-action-forced-labor-section-301-investigations" target="_blank" >counts</a> "60 economies," but that includes the European Union, which encompasses 27 countries, so the actual number is 86, accounting for nearly all U.S. imports, which will be taxed at either 10% or 12.5%.</p><p>According to a <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/002-Burlap-and-Barrel-v.-Greer-Compl-2026-07-24.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> that the Liberty Justice Center <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/pressrelease/liberty-justice-center-challenges-unlawful-section-301-tariffs-as-administration-replaces-expiring-section-122-tariffs/" target="_blank" >filed</a> last week on behalf of the U.S. businesses that will have to pay the Section 301 tariffs, the findings underlying Greer's list are woefully inadequate. By and large, they fail to specify exactly how each of these countries has fallen short, how their supposed failures burden U.S. commerce, or why the new tariffs, which make no distinction between forced-labor products and other imports, can be expected to ameliorate the problem that the administration claims to be addressing.</p><p>The Liberty Justice Center complaint argues that the forced-labor issue is "simply a pretext" for reinstating Trump's "invalidated global tariff regime." That impression is confirmed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's <a class="Link" href="https://www.c-span.org/clip/public-affairs-event/treasury-secretary-says-2026-tariff-revenue-will-remain-virtually-unchanged-after-supreme-court-ruling/5193748" target="_blank" >assurance</a> of "virtually unchanged tariff revenue," his <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/podcasts/opinion-potomac-watch/paul-gigot-in-conversation-with-us-treasury-secretary-scott-bessent/ce6e45f7-9a20-4ba9-b0be-98a33021623f" target="_blank" >statement</a> that Greer's "Section 301 studies" would result in "tariffs at the previous level," and Greer's <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/february/ambassador-greer-issues-statement-supreme-court-ieepa-decision" target="_blank" >promise</a> that the new taxes would "address many of the issues at the heart of the President's reciprocal tariff program."</p><p>This strategy, the Liberty Justice Center says, is inconsistent with Section 301, which was designed as a remedy for specific practices by specific trading partners, as opposed to an excuse for broad tariffs aimed at reducing the gap between imported and exported goods. Interpreting Section 301 to justify the latter, the center warns, would violate the "major questions" doctrine, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12077" target="_blank" >requires</a> clear congressional authorization for policies of "vast economic and political significance," and allow an <a class="Link" href="https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S1-5-1/ALDE_00000014/" target="_blank" >unconstitutional delegation</a> of legislative powers.</p><p>That lawsuit may not be a slam dunk. But since the Liberty Justice Center spearheaded the successful challenge to Trump's International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariffs, the president should be worried.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-640000" name="module-640000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Wife wouldn't be counted among musician's biggest fans
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I have been married 31 years. We have a great marriage. We work from home, so we spend pretty much every minute together and enjoy each other's company so much that it isn't an issue. That said, I will also share that I'm a basement musician. It's my hobby. I play guitar and sing. In the past, I have appeared in bands as well as solo formats. I'm also a pretty good songwriter. I have written a number of songs, including several about my wife and the love we share.</p><p>My challenge is that my wife isn't very musical. She can go days at a time without listening to any music at all. In the big scheme of things, this might not sound like a huge deal. I am cool with it. But in all our 31 years together, she has never asked me to play anything for her — none of the songs I have written for her or covers of famous songs.</p><p>I have pointed this fact out to her more than once, hoping to drop a hint that, even if she doesn't appreciate music, asking me to sing one of those songs for her would make me feel like she appreciated the effort and thought. When friends and family ask me to play them, she always says she likes them, but the requests never come from her. Am I asking too much to expect it, or should I just let it go and stop writing them? — <i>STILL WAITING IN VIRGINIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR STILL WAITING:</b> Face it — the woman you married 31 years ago has never been a music lover, regardless of who the composer is. However, writing songs about your feelings is a form of free expression, and I don't think you should quit doing it if it's satisfying for you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a single, retired female. I have a personal side business that keeps me quite busy, and I'm blessed to have many friends. I am also active in community and church events. My issue is that a lot of my friends who are inactive and retired invite me to dinners, the theater and parties, sometimes at the very last minute. Then they become annoyed when I decline. They also endlessly keep me tied up on the phone or on text messages with utter nonsense.</p><p>I am a people-pleaser and feel bad when I must decline an invitation. I have proper manners and know etiquette, but this has become frustrating and annoying. I have endlessly responded with, "I would love to go, but I need advance notice," to no avail. What to do? — <i>PERPLEXED IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR PERPLEXED:</b> Because you are a people-pleaser and want to offend no one, continue responding as you already do, "I'd love to go, but I need more advance notice than you have given me." While you're at it, it isn't rude to be too busy to chat if someone calls at an inopportune time. (You can always screen your calls if they are oppressive, and take your time responding to their texts.)</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To order "How to Write Letters for All Occasions," send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby — Letter Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Trump is our cold-blooded leader
entries.summary: <p>The feature film "Pressure," starring Brendan Fraser as a fierce but principled General Dwight D. Eisenhower conflicted about whether and when to invade Normandy, has disturbing relevance for the current plight of our nation.</p><p>So heavy was the burden Ike felt in 1944 from putting the lives of American boys at risk that he wrote a historically famous “in case I fail” note ahead of time, essentially apologizing and assuming full responsibility for lost lives were the invasion to fail.</p><p>When D-Day succeeded in turning the tide of the war, Ike discarded the note, which was later salvaged for posterity by an aide. But even after the war ended, historians noted how the empathic general, subsequently elected president and commander-in-chief, was forever saddened and conscience-plagued by every U.S. soldier who died under his command.</p><p>The calculus of lives lost weighs considerably on nearly all presidents, not just as commander of the armed forces, but also because of the immense power they wield that affects the lives of so many human beings.</p><p>Yet our current president seems unfazed by the jeopardy in which he places people, in view of the frightful number of deaths resulting from his policies and decisions.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4b0000" name="module-4b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Start with, for example, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island, and Alex Pretti and Renée Good in Minneapolis, all of whom were fatally shot by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. At least one shooting suggests agents were <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/homan-ice-vetting-maine-12246122" target="_blank" >poorly trained</a>. In another, ICE agents <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/09/us/lorenzo-salgado-araujo-houston-ice-shooting" target="_blank" >targeted</a> the wrong person. In yet another, agents were shown on <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/02/13/nx-s1-5713947/immigration-agents-lie-minnesota" target="_blank" >video</a> to be lying in their self-defense claims.</p><p>The federal agents were let loose in American cities and told they had total immunity in going after immigrants by <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/DHSgov/status/2011213308968538361?lang=en" target="_blank" >Stephen Miller</a>, the vampiric hireling of Donald Trump who has neither apologized nor unmasked his storm troopers.</p><h3>Questionable strikes</h3><h3></h3><p>Equally egregious has been the slaughter of <a class="Link" href="https://www.theatlantic.com/national-security/2026/07/trump-narcoterrorists-boat-strikes/687763/" target="_blank" >221 lives</a> in 61 boat strikes in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, ordered by Trump, alleging with no proof whatsoever that they were transporting drugs. Even more cold-blooded, if possible, were the follow-up strikes to finish off <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/boat-strike-survivors-hegseth-congress-legal-details-ce16f4740841b2b5f2904588335a818e" target="_blank" >distressed sailors</a> clinging to wreckage in the water and begging to surrender.</p><p>Such violations of international law, aka war crimes, seemed to have set a precedent for the mass killing of 175 Iranian civilians, including<a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/policy/defense/5967941-democratic-senators-report-iran-school-strike/" target="_blank" > 54 young schoolchildren</a>, by an American Tomahawk missile at the start of Trump’s war with Iran, for which he, again, offered <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/16/opinion/trump-minab-civilian-casualties-iran-war.html?unlocked_article_code=1.1lA.goJ3.iZoctueK2cKB&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >no apology</a>, and didn't even acknowledge. The horrendous, avoidable tragedy only happened because Trump chose to go to war, absent congressional approval, absent popular support, absent any consistent rationale, and absent a solid reason save for a twisted notion of personal glory for notching a wartime victory. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/article/us-soldiers-killed-iran-war.html?unlocked_article_code=1.1lA.8ANv.VtKn3gZLKYYy&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >Seventeen</a> American troops have been killed so far, including three last week.</p><h3></h3><p>Trump was blamed by the British journal the Lancet for hundreds of thousands of <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/538400-lancet-report-faults-trump-for-avoidable-coronavirus-deaths/" target="_blank" >unnecessary deaths</a> in the U.S. from COVID-19 during his first term because of his irresponsible delay in telling the American people about the pandemic, followed by his administration’s disjointed national response, its indecisiveness and its scientifically dubious recommendations for drugs, cures, masks, social distancing and indoor rallies, all in an effort to downplay the crisis for political advantage.</p><p>Through both terms, his executive orders reversing workplace and environmental protections for corporate interests have resulted in tens of thousands of deaths from diseases caused by air and water pollution. The Lancet reported that 22,000 deaths in 2019 were tied to regulatory rollbacks. </p><h3>How is this serving the people?</h3><h3></h3><p>Meanwhile, tons of extra greenhouse gases emitted because of Trump’s removal of the U.S. from the Paris Agreement and his regressive orders to undo mitigation measures for global warming are projected by experts to cause an estimated <a class="Link" href="https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-climate-rollbacks-heat-deaths" target="_blank" >1.3 million</a> needless temperature-related deaths in the next several decades, according to a joint report by ProPublica and the Guardian.</p><p>Coddling the National Rifle Association and gun manufacturers, Trump has done nothing to regulate firearms and reduce school shootings, while rolling back existing regulations. In his first term, gun homicides increased by 34%, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://giffords.org/press-release/2025/03/trump-administration-deletes-surgeon-general-webpage-with-advisory-on-gun-violence/" target="_blank" >Giffords</a> PAC. </p><p>His One Big Beautiful Bill cutting subsidies to healthcare, and his mission to end medical research funding to universities he does not like, will kill millions more deprived of potential cures for various cancers.</p><p>Thousands have been sickened by measles and other preventable diseases because of public mistrust of vaccines, which is directly attributable to the anti-vaccine advocacy by the administration’s health department and Trump’s anti-vaccination health and human services secretary, Robert Kennedy Jr.</p><p>So much death, for which this president is unapologetic, as he exhibits a "let them eat cake" indifference and dwells, instead, on his ballroom, arch and delusions about the 2020 election.</p><p>When Trump is gone, and historians characterize his legacy, he will be known more as an agent of the Grim Reaper than a president who served the people.</p><p><i>David McGrath is an emeritus English professor at College of DuPage and author of “</i><a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/Far-Enough-Away-David-McGrath-ebook/dp/B0CPNSTWMG#:~:text=Book%20overview,are%20not%20Irish%2C%20after%20all" target="_blank" ><i>Far Enough Away</i></a><i>,” a collection of Chicago area stories.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cc0000" name="module-cc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
