entries.title: Senate finally starts defying Trump
entries.summary: <p>At the start of Donald Trump’s second term, the Senate had a very important job: provide advice and consent on the newly elected president’s Cabinet picks, as enumerated in Article II, Section 2, Clause 2 of the U.S. Constitution.</p><p>These hearings don’t always come with fireworks, controversy and drama — in 2017, for example, all but one of Trump’s nominations were confirmed. In 2021, all but one of Joe Biden’s picks were confirmed.</p><p>But in all fairness, neither 2017 nor 2021 was the wild and wacky clown show of 2025.</p><p>Trump’s second-term Cabinet reads like a list of who’s who of questionable and unsavory characters from the quackiest corners of the MAGA mediasphere.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>There was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose “Fox & Friends” weekend co-host gig may have gotten him the job, but whose personal life — accusations of infidelity, sexual assault and alcohol abuse — became a humiliating and alarming side story that nearly derailed his confirmation. Emphasis on “nearly.”</p><p>There was Justice Department head Pam Bondi, who had actively worked to undermine the 2020 election results, had faced accusations of corruption while Florida attorney general and was presumed to be a willing accomplice in Trump’s efforts to weaponize the DOJ against his political enemies.</p><p>There was Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a known science-denier and conspiracy theorist whose weird interactions with a <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2024/08/05/nx-s1-5063939/rfk-jr-central-park-bear-bicycle" target="_blank" >dead bear</a>, a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2024/07/02/politics/rfk-jr-eating-dog-vanity-fair" target="_blank" >dead dog</a>, a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2024/07/02/politics/rfk-jr-eating-dog-vanity-fair" target="_blank" >dead brain worm</a>— and a <a class="Link" href="https://www.status.news/p/olivia-nuzzi-rfk-new-york-magazine" target="_blank" >living New York magazine reporter</a>— very much should have ended his confirmation bid.</p><p>And let’s not forget Tulsi Gabbard, Kash Patel, Kristi Noem and Howard Lutnick — a “Star Wars” bar of unqualified, attention-seeking sycophants who definitely weren’t “the best people.”</p><p>But every one was confirmed, in many cases with every Republican voting yes — <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/senate-vote-trump-cabinet-picks-top-nominees/" target="_blank" >only five</a> of the 53 Republicans voted against at least one of the president’s nominees, despite their clear and concerning controversies. It was an embarrassing look for the upper chamber.</p><p>But what a difference a year — and a midterm election — makes.</p><p>The Senate seems to have finally found its voice in standing up to Trump as he — and maybe because he — actively imperils their majority with every primary challenge, impolitic distraction, and election denial he offers.</p><p>Sen. Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has resisted pressure from Trump to eliminate the 60-vote legislative filibuster, and is now <a class="Link" href="https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/americas/us-politics/thune-trump-senate-voter-id-b3020589.html" target="_blank" >openly stating his frustration</a> with Trump’s demands that Republicans pass his election-denialism Safeguard American Voter Eligibility, or SAVE America Act, telling Trump to “get on the phone and get the votes.”</p><p>Despite Trump’s insistence, <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/30/john-thune-trump-pressure-senate-01016783" target="_blank" >Thune is pushing</a> for senators to go home so they can campaign for their reelections, something Trump seems wholly disinterested in.</p><p>Meanwhile, retiring Sens. Thom Tillis, R-Texas<b>,</b> and John Cornyn, R-N.C., — both victims of Trump’s capricious and needless primarying — have held up his nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general, insisting Blanche provide a written guarantee the administration will not pursue a $1.8 billion weaponization slush fund.</p><p>Trump, who can only afford to lose one Republican vote, said Thursday that he may withdraw Blanche’s name until Tillis and Cornyn are out of office next year.</p><p>Three other Republicans — Bill Cassidy, R-La., Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska — banded together to oppose Bill Pulte’s appointment to be director of national intelligence, effectively forcing Trump to give up.</p><p>And a group of Republicans, including Cassidy and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., joined Democrats to limit Trump’s unilateral war powers, hoping to force an ending to his unpopular, ill-advised and spiraling Iran war adventure.</p><p>It’s perhaps a taste of the continued pressure Trump may face from his own party in his lame-duck years, or maybe it’s a foreshadowing of his life under a Democratic majority if Republicans get voted out in November.</p><p>But either way, it’s a welcome sight — senators, finally doing the job they were elected to do.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Trump isn't funny — just mean
entries.summary: <p>In a display of Stockholm Syndrome, the White House Correspondents' Association invited Donald Trump to be the keynote speaker at their annual festival of self-appreciation. Because he is who he is, he did not take the opportunity to do the kind of gentle press ribbing that past presidents have engaged in, and he certainly declined to engage in the self-deprecating humor that charmed audiences in the old days. Instead, he delivered a string of puerile insults that would be beneath a fifth grader.</p><p>The tuxedo and ball gown-clad lads and ladies were forced to sit through meandering gibberish about the White House UFC fight, the weather forecast, the White House ballroom, why he hadn't attended the Correspondents' Association dinner in the past and how "hot" America is now. Then he let loose with a string of gross insults:</p><p>"But I can exclusively reveal to you this evening that for the heaviest of the heavyweights, we will have Sloppy Chris Christie, one of the sloppiest human beings you'll ever meet. Fighting, I would say, I could mention the governor of Chicago (sic), but I'm going to mention instead Jerry Nadler. And they're fighting for a big piece of cheesecake, big fat piece of cheesecake.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c70000" name="module-c70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>"But we had a contest for who had the lowest ratings and the lowest IQ on television. And that was actually Don Lemon, I think. When I said that he's the dumbest man on television, I said, 'When you say some things, you never make a comeback.'</p><p>"But this year, the association decided not to have a comedian. So they considered using Jimmy Kimmel. Jimmy Fallon. These guys, they're terrible. They're terrible. Stephen Colbert, these are people without talent. They get a lot. They have talent. You know who has talent? Their agent getting them the money they get. They have no talent. But they are not comedians. They're not funny people. They're angry people. They're sick people."</p><p>The president also noted that he "hated ... Adam 'Shifty' Schiff," calling him "a terrible person. He's a liar. And I called him Watermelon Head because he is the largest head I've ever seen with the smallest neck, pencil neck. How does that big, fat, ugly head stand on a little pencil neck?"</p><p>Why dwell on this? Because many people, even those who abhor Trump, say he's funny.</p><p>I confess I've never seen the evidence. People often laugh at transgression. It's not that they find it funny (though some may) but that laughter is often a reaction to surprise. I've noticed in meetings that when people use the f-bomb, others tend to smile, not because it's funny but because it's surprising in the circumstances (or at least it used to be before the f-word became the all-purpose placeholder in modern speech).</p><p>So perhaps Trump's gross insults and vile jibes evoke a certain shock and therefore laughter? I don't know. Certainly, some of his fans enjoy the grossness and cruelty, but that ain't wit.</p><h3><b>Other leaders made Americans laugh</b></h3><p>We have seen wit in politicians in the past, and one must wonder whether our age would even recognize the real thing.</p><p>Sen. Bob Dole, R-Kan., who was crippled fighting in Italy during World War II, had a deadpan delivery. After he received just 607 votes in the 1980 New Hampshire Republican presidential primary, he said, "The day after New Hampshire, I went home and slept like a baby. Every two hours I woke up and cried." He coined the much-repeated line "The most dangerous place to be in Washington is between Chuck Schumer and a TV camera."</p><p>Others did self-deprecating humor with grace. George W. Bush performed an 11-minute routine alongside Steve Bridges, a hilarious Bush impersonator. Both poked fun at the president's malapropisms and poor pronunciation.</p><p>Several years later, Barack Obama invited Keegan-Michael Key to be his "anger translator." While not quite as self-effacing as Bush's skit, it did poke fun at Obama's cerebral, detached, sometimes even robotic delivery.</p><p>Running against World War II hero Dwight Eisenhower cannot have been easy. But Adlai Stevenson brought a certain elan to the task. In a 1952 Fresno speech, he said, "I have been thinking that I would make a proposition to my Republican friends ... that if they will stop telling lies about the Democrats, we will stop telling the truth about them." On another occasion, when a supporter approached him and declared, "You are every thinking man's candidate," he replied, "Thank you madam, but I require a majority."</p><p>When Dick Tuck lost a California state senate primary, he called a press conference and deadpanned, "The people have spoken — the bastards." Rep. Mo Udall, D-Ariz., later borrowed that line and also quipped that "the only cure for presidential fever is embalming fluid."</p><p>New York Mayor Ed Koch offered a variation on Tuck's theme when he lost reelection in 1989: "The people have spoken ... and they must be punished."</p><p>Republican Sen. Alan Simpson, Wyoming's unfailing wag, once described the political parties this way: "We have two political parties in this country, the Stupid Party and the Evil Party. I belong to the Stupid Party." He also said, "Those who travel the high road of humility are not troubled by heavy traffic."</p><p>And the frequently droll Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., responding to a young man who asked whether he wasn't too old to run for president (he was 63), quipped, "Thanks for the question you little jerk." That was tart but not cruel, because the point was that the question had hit a nerve.</p><p>I don't know about you, but I would give a lot for a politician of genuine wit right now.</p><p>Trump said the White House Correspondents' Association didn't hire a comedian this year. True, but they did invite a clown.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bf0000" name="module-bf0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Women's pro baseball comes home to Illinois, paving the way for next generation of ballplayers
entries.summary: <p>Seven years ago, 11-year-old Amira Hondras made a list of goals for her baseball career. The biggest among them was making the women's national team and playing professionally.</p><p>Around then, she competed at Rivets Stadium in Rockford in the Baseball for All national tournament, which hosts an annual international youth girls’ baseball contest for ages eight to 18.</p><p>She returned to Rivets last weekend, this time on the roster of the U.S. national women's baseball team, which closed out the weekend undefeated in the qualifying round of the Women's Baseball World Cup. It secured them a ticket back to Rockford for the international tournament's finals next year.</p><p>This Saturday, the 18-year-old will bat for the L.A. Queens as they face the New York Heights at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield for the Women's Professional Baseball League's opening day.</p><p>Hondras' loved ones already made the 100-mile trip from the south suburbs with a cardboard cut-out of her face to cheer her on last weekend, and plan to continue through the WPBL season.</p><p>And it's all taking place in Illinois — where women's baseball flourished more than 70 years ago — as a new generation of professional players steps up.</p><p>"I don’t think it gets more full circle than that,” Hondras told the Sun-Times. “This could be anywhere in the world, and having that support there in the stands makes the experience so much better. It makes it feel like home.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-540000" team 22-2 in the Women’s Baseball World Cup in Rockford on July 22.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>World Baseball Softball Confederation</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Women's Baseball World Cup is an international competition held every three years since 2004, filling the gap left by the lack of an Olympic category for women's baseball.</p><p>The WPBL aims to take up the mantle of its ancestor, the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, which got its start in Chicago in 1943. Tryouts for teams like the Rockford Peaches, famously depicted in the 1992 movie and 2022 television show "A League of Their Own," were first held at Wrigley Field that year. The AAGBPL shut down in 1954.</p><p>Other U.S.-based professional women's baseball leagues came and went in the years since. The last was the short-lived Ladies Professional Baseball League, which was shut down in its second season in 1998.</p><p>Hondras, the lone Chicago player in the league, grew up in a baseball family of Sox fans on the South Side, and eventually, South Holland.</p><p>By age 12, she was selected as the first girl in the White Sox Amateur City Elite youth baseball team. She played there until she was picked up by the national team and subsequently the professional league.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/07/25/a-ray-of-sunshine-with-basketballs-wnba-all-star-weekend-lights-up-chicago" >‘A ray of sunshine with basketballs': WNBA All-Star Weekend lights up Chicago</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/01/29/womens-sports-fans-bar-lakeview-flores-level-sporting-club" >Women’s sports fans will have a new place to hang out with opening of Level Sporting Club</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But Hondras' path to professional baseball hasn't always existed.</p><p>Growing up in the 1960s, Kat Williams often took part in neighborhood sandlot pickup games; it was her only avenue to play baseball. Her admiration for the sport carried on as she played through the years, though never on a team.</p><p>She helped found the International Women’s Baseball Center in 2012. entries.title: After decades behind bars, Ivy Kelly was given a choice: Walk free, or keep fighting to clear his name
entries.summary: <p>Inside the Cook County Jail’s “super max” division, Ivy Kelly goes about his daily shift, serving lunch to fellow detainees, until correctional officers interrupt him.</p><p>The officers escort Kelly to a cramped room where detainees meet with their lawyers. Today, there’s no lawyer — just me and a photographer.</p><p>Kelly, 51, sits across from us. His hair is short, parted and styled into waves. He wears eyeglasses with a dark browline. He looks bookish. No nonsense.</p><p>Kelly has always insisted he’s innocent of the 1999 killing that led to his decades-long prison sentence.</p><p>In 2014, an appeals court raised doubts about his trial’s fairness. Eventually, prosecutors made Kelly an offer: He could walk free — if he just admitted guilt.</p><p>We’ve spoken a couple times online, but I’ve come to the jail to ask in person about his response to the offer — a response that has weighed heavily ever since.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>WBEZ’s Chip Mitchell records Ivy Kelly in a jail corridor after their interview in a cramped room where detainees meet with their lawyers. Kelly spoke of his response to a 2022 offer from Cook County prosecutors to enable his immediate release if he admitted guilt in the murder of a man he calls his best friend. Kelly’s decision has weighed heavily since.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>We don’t have much time in the jail room. So I proceed chronologically, starting with his connection to the murder victim, Joe Ward.</p><p>Kelly says they met as students at Polaris, a former college-prep high school in Oak Lawn.</p><p>“He became, actually, my best friend,” he says.</p><p>Kelly needed a best friend. He says his stepfather was abusive to him and his mother.</p><p>“My mom also had an abusive childhood,” Kelly says. “I understood why she probably allowed things to go on, probably fearful for her own safety at times.”</p><p>Throughout high school, Kelly bounced among their home, his grandmother’s place and an aunt’s house.</p><p>Some nights, when he had nowhere else to go, he’d sleep in a car.</p><p>Other times, Ward took him in.</p><p>“He would sneak me into his basement,” Kelly says. “His mom would come down in the morning. She would just look at me because we’d never asked, ‘Could I spend the night?’”</p><p>Then, she would go up to the kitchen and feed him breakfast, just like her own kids, he says.</p><p>Kelly managed to graduate from high school. Later, in trade school, he learned about heating, ventilation and air conditioning. And he had five kids.</p><p>But he was convicted of a felony for firing a gun during what Kelly says was an altercation. And he dealt drugs — with Ward.</p><p>“The plan was to start buying and rehabbing houses so that we could stop selling drugs,” Kelly says.</p><p>That plan went off the rails on Dec. 10, 1999, when two men approached Ward outside a Robbins house. At least one fired shots, killing him.</p><p>More than three months later, Robbins police officers arrested Kelly and another man. They were charged with Ward’s murder. Prosecutors said Kelly was tired of Ward pestering him to settle a drug debt. They had statements from two purported eyewitnesses identifying Kelly as a shooter.</p><p>Kelly countered that he was blocks away at the time of the shooting. But both men were convicted. Kelly was sentenced to 30 years in prison.</p><p>He ended up at Menard Correctional Center, 340 miles south of Chicago. That maximum-security prison, built in the 19th century, is known for poor conditions.</p><p>There, Kelly kept fighting to clear his name. He found a fellow inmate who knew how to prepare and file a petition to challenge a conviction.</p><p>“I came back to him, and I asked him, ‘What do I owe you?’ And he said, ‘You got a bag of coffee?’” Kelly says. “Somebody who cared enough to help me, all he wanted was a bag of Maxwell House coffee that cost a buck-forty.”</p><p>In the filing, Kelly argued that his trial lawyer had made mistakes so severe they violated his constitutional rights. The lawyer, when I reached him, admitted the errors. He chalked them up to early-career inexperience with murder cases.</p><p>The errors included failing to question one of the eyewitnesses about a criminal case of his own and about having been paid by the federal government to provide information. Such questioning would have raised doubts about the credibility of that witness.</p><p>Kelly later accused prosecutors of hiding exculpatory evidence, including contemporaneous reports about the killing written by the Robbins detective in charge of the case. The detective, Jerome McGee, pleaded guilty in 2001 to a federal racketeering charge for taking cash to protect a drug dealer. He spent more than six years in prison.</p><p>Kelly also accused prosecutors of hiding a 1999 assault charge against the Robbins officer who replaced McGee as the murder case’s lead detective.</p><p>“Why withhold the detective’s background?” Kelly says.</p><p>The prosecutors said they didn’t withhold anything material to the murder case.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-870000" name="image-870000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5d16a37/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4d43aab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/403a4fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Cook County Jail 2600 S. California. Thursday, March 22, 2012 | Brian Jackson~Sun-Times." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/403a4fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/753fdb4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/403a4fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+94/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F38%2F62b10d0b9cbd92cedc3b9a63c5a3%2Fdivision-9-cook-county.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cook County Jail’s Division 9 holds detainees including Ivy Kelly in two maximum-security buildings near South Sacramento Avenue and West 31st Street. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So there was Kelly in prison, convicted years earlier of killing a man he calls his best friend. He kept trying to prove his innocence. Eventually, his claim gained traction, leading to a gut-wrenching decision.</p><p>Here is how the decision went down.</p><p>The 2014 appellate ruling required Cook County Circuit Judge Michele M. Pitman, a former prosecutor, to hold an evidentiary hearing on whether Kelly was entitled to a retrial.</p><p>In 2022, as that hearing finally drew near, prosecutors offered Kelly a deal. They would agree to a sentence reduction of nearly eight years. He could get out of prison immediately. But only if he admitted guilt in the shooting.</p><p>This sort of bargaining leads many pretrial defendants to plead guilty in exchange for a lighter sentence.</p><p>But the dealmaking can also happen years after a conviction — before a post-conviction hearing or before a retrial.</p><p>More often than not, experts say, the person who's locked up takes the offer. One study examined 250 cases across the country from 2010 to 2020. In each case, a <i>pro bono</i> group had agreed to represent someone trying to overturn a conviction for a serious crime, such as murder or rape.</p><p>“The cases go through extremely rigorous vetting,” says University of Wisconsin law professor emeritus Keith Findley, who led the study. “The groups only spend their resources on … really powerful claims of actual innocence.”</p><p>The study found that nearly a quarter of the claimants were offered a sentence-reduction deal — typically allowing them to go free immediately in exchange for admitting guilt, like the offer to Kelly.</p><p>Of those claimants, Findley says, 59% “succumbed to the pressures” and took the deal.</p><p>When the prosecutors in Kelly’s case informed Pitman they had offered him a deal for immediate release, the judge ordered him to stand before her.</p><p>“I want to make sure the record is clear,” Pitman told him, according to the court transcript.</p><p>“We don’t know what’s going to happen with this hearing,” the judge said, referring to the post-conviction proceeding, not mentioning the years it could take from there to get a retrial. “The state is telling me they’ve tendered you an offer today for time served on this case. Is that correct?”</p><p>“Yes, ma’am,” Kelly answered.</p><p>“And have you considered that offer, sir?”</p><p>“I’m innocent.”</p><p>“My question is: Have you considered that offer?” the judge pressed Kelly, stressing that, if he took the deal, he “would be released today.”</p><p>“Yes, ma’am.”</p><p>“And you’ve talked about that with your attorneys?”</p><p>“Yes, ma’am.”</p><p>“And it’s your desire to reject the offer for time served?” Pitman asked.</p><p>“Yes, ma’am.”</p><p>In 2023, almost a year later, the judge threw out Kelly’s conviction.</p><p>But prosecutors under then-Cook County State’s Attorney Kim Foxx decided not to drop the charges. They would retry him for the killing and, until then, he'd have to remain behind bars because, they argued, he was a safety menace.</p><p>Kelly says he could not understand that.</p><p>“They argued that I was a threat to the community, a threat to a witness, and the judge ordered me detained,” Kelly says. “I was confused the whole time because I’m not dangerous if I plead guilty, but I’m dangerous because I maintain my innocence.”</p><p>Under State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, Foxx’s successor, prosecutors have stuck with pursuing the murder charges and keeping Kelly in jail.</p><p>I asked O’Neill Burke’s office why prosecutors consider Kelly more dangerous for fighting to clear his name. A spokesperson responded there would be no comment on a pending case.</p><p>Foxx, who stepped down as state’s attorney in 2024, says she has “no recollection of this matter.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ff0000" name="image-ff0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e4d87a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c17f33/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ac6a40/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke answers questions during a news conference at the George N. Leighton Criminal Courthouse in Little Village, Wednesday, Aug. 13, 2025, where she announced no charges against police officers who shot and killed Dexter Reed during a traffic stop in 2024. | Pat Nabong/Sun-Times" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ac6a40/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6030e11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ac6a40/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F28%2F4ae078244a06ae3d6e1e0190f5e2%2Feobcharges-081425-14.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Prosecutors under Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke have stuck behind Ivy Kelly’s murder charges and his detainment since a judge tossed out his conviction.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>By the time the conviction was thrown out, Kelly had been moved to Dixon Correctional Center, 100 miles west of Chicago, putting him closer to friends and family. Years of good behavior behind bars had led to minimum-security status, he says.</p><p>“It was like a college campus,” Kelly says.</p><p>Pending a retrial, though, the judge ordered him moved to the Cook County Jail.</p><p>Kelly says he was first put in a detox unit full of drug addicts — dozens to a room, most in withdrawal.</p><p>Then, he was moved to the jail's Division 9, where he has had to put up with young men charged with serious crimes.</p><p>“It’s the worst division in the county jail,” he says.</p><p>At one point, Kelly found out his mother had cancer. And, less than three months after his transfer from prison to the jail, she died.</p><p>It was all too much for him.</p><p>The plea offer was still on the table, according to Kelly’s attorneys. Ahead of his mother’s funeral, he says he considered taking it.</p><p>“I was ready to give up then,” Kelly says, voice faltering and eyes welling with tears. “I was ready to just give up and go home so I could be there when they buried her.”</p><p>But he says his lawyer and friends all told him the same thing: “You’re strong. You got to keep fighting. You came all this way. They stole a quarter century of your life. You can’t just give up like that.”</p><p>He knew the fight for exoneration could keep him behind bars for years longer. But again he dug in.</p><p>“I want to go home. I miss my kids. I’m estranged from my kids now. But, at the same token, I know I’m innocent,” Kelly says. “If I got to sit, I got to sit.”</p><p>Kelly has been locked up for 26 years.</p><p>His retrial is set for Nov. 2. He knows he might lose. If he does, he might not get out of prison until 2030.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2c0000" name="image-2c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2d5b2bc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F9b%2Fd9c347424f0bb81058d7863c182f%2Fwatchivykelly-260628-39.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/892450e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F9b%2Fd9c347424f0bb81058d7863c182f%2Fwatchivykelly-260628-39.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd48f53/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2F9b%2Fd9c347424f0bb81058d7863c182f%2Fwatchivykelly-260628-39.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ivy Kelly, who is incarcerated at Division 9 of the Cook County Department of Corrections and maintains his innocence after serving 26 years, walks to the elevator before resuming his work inside the jail, Friday, June 12, 2026. entries.title: Cook County predicts charity care will soar to highest level in more than a decade
entries.summary: <p>Cook County Health expects to provide around $485 million in free or discounted care next year, returning to an era before the Affordable Care Act insured millions more Americans than it does today.</p><p>That’s about $100 million more in what’s known as charity care than the county expects to provide this year, and the largest amount in more than a decade.</p><p>What’s largely driving this is people losing health insurance — people with low incomes in particular. That’s less money flowing to Cook County Health, which mostly treats poor and immigrant patients at its two hospitals, John H. Stroger Jr. and Provident, and more than a dozen community health centers.</p><p>In 2027, the health system expects about 30% of its patients to be uninsured — more than double a 13% low in 2023.</p><p>Dr. Erik Mikaitis, CEO of Cook County Health, sees the ripple effects reaching beyond the hospitals and health centers he oversees into communities and even into businesses, when sick people can’t work.</p><p>“If you don’t have insurance, you’re less likely to engage,” Mikaitis said in an interview with WBEZ before unveiling his proposed 2027 budget. “You’re going to come to the ED with a stroke or a heart attack instead of going to the clinic to manage your blood pressure.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-da0000" name="html-embed-module-da0000"></a><div style="min-height:551px" id="datawrapper-vis-lyXCG"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lyXCG/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-lyXCG"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lyXCG/full.png" alt="Charity care at Cook County Health is expected to reach its highest level in more than a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Cook County Health is one of the biggest public health systems in the nation. The estimated spike in charity care for low-income people is part of the health system’s preliminary $4.7 billion budget for 2027. It’s a slimmer budget by more than $400 million compared to this year. That’s partly from cutting costs to get ahead of not bringing in as much money, but also because the health system’s Medicaid health insurance plan, CountyCare, is expected to be smaller next year based on about 50,000 current members losing coverage.</p><p>Mikaitis is focused on making sure insurers pay the health system for all the treatment it bills for, and helping low-income patients with Medicaid <a class="Link" href="https://cookcountyhealth.org/press-release/get-medicaid-facts-new-site-and-toolkit-launched-to-educate-public-about-looming-medicaid-eligibility-changes/" target="_blank" ><u>keep their coverage</u></a> despite new roadblocks from Washington.</p><p>Next year, <a class="Link" href="https://cookcountyhealth.org/press-release/get-medicaid-facts-new-site-and-toolkit-launched-to-educate-public-about-looming-medicaid-eligibility-changes/" target="_blank" ><u>big cuts to Medicaid</u></a> public health insurance for people who are poor or have disabilities take effect. <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/medicaidfedpolicychfs.html" target="_blank" ><u>New work requirements kick in</u></a> as well as more frequent checks to make sure people qualify.</p><p>In Illinois, around one in four people have Medicaid. More than 400,000 people <a class="Link" href="https://www.rwjf.org/en/insights/our-research/2026/03/millions-could-lose-health-coverage-due-to-new-rules.html" target="_blank" ><u>could lose coverage</u></a>, and around half of them live in Cook County.</p><p>Mikaitis still plans to make some investments at Cook County Health, such as upgrading MRIs. There are no plans for layoffs or cuts to service for patients, but that depends on if the health system can receive $40 million from the county to close an estimated gap, Mikaitis said. Otherwise, around 150 people could be let go, as well as cuts to medical care and other programs that help patients, like research and housing assistance.</p><p>“We’ve essentially cut to the bone at this point,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-530000" name="image-530000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d3a587c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1b998b9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f59f220/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Dr. Erik Mikaitis, CEO of Cook County Health, speaks during a news conference at John H. Stroger, Jr. Hospital of Cook County in the Illinois Medical District." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f59f220/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ac78252/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f59f220/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6488x3641+0+342/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F13%2Ff2857eb14dff88c26519587abf06%2Fcovidshot-092124-11-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dr. Erik Mikaitis, CEO of Cook County Health, says the health system needs $40 million from the county to close an estimated budget gap or else it will have to turn to cuts and layoffs.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A bigger question is how much the health system’s finances <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2025/05/23/how-medicaid-cuts-from-congress-could-affect-every-cook-county-resident" target="_blank" ><u>could affect the county’s</u></a> overall bottom line and other services the county provides for all residents, from getting property tax bills on time to running the county’s vast court system and jail. The health system is one of the biggest pieces of the county’s overall budget.</p><p>A spokesperson for Cook County Board Toni Preckwinkle said it’s too early to discuss.</p><p>“We’re working through the budget process and we’re well aware of the financial challenges ahead,” spokeswoman Cara Yi said.</p><p>The health system’s budget eventually becomes part of the overall county budget. Preckwinkle typically pitches her proposal to county commissioners in October, who must approve it. The new budget takes effect Dec. 1.</p><p>What’s happening at Cook County Health is likely to play out in communities across the U.S.</p><p>Besides <a class="Link" href="https://cookcountyhealth.org/press-release/get-medicaid-facts-new-site-and-toolkit-launched-to-educate-public-about-looming-medicaid-eligibility-changes/" target="_blank" ><u>Medicaid</u></a> cuts, other people are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/24/obamacare-health-insurance-illinois-aca-tax-subsidies" target="_blank" ><u>dropping plans</u></a> they bought on government health insurance exchanges they no longer can afford now that enhanced ACA subsidies have disappeared after Congress let them lapse last year.</p><p>The pressure compounds. Cuts to other government-funded programs like federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" target="_blank" ><u>food assistance</u></a> could lead to poorer health in a community, while other hospitals and clinics facing the same stress could cut back services or close — potentially sending more patients to the county.</p><p>“That’s going to have, I'm really concerned, a devastating impact on the current hospitals that are struggling,” Mikaitis said. “Those patients have to go somewhere, right?”</p><p>Two safety-net hospitals in the Chicago area, which largely treat low-income patients like Cook County Health, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>shuttered in the last year</u></a>. Others are on the bubble now, Mikaitis said, even before the Medicaid cuts start. In some cases these hospitals have received advances not just <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>from the state</u></a> but <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/health-care/ccb-roseland-health-grant-making-payroll-20260722/" target="_blank" ><u>from CountyCare</u></a> to help make ends meet.</p><p>All of these changes could affect people who never step inside a safety net hospital, Mikaitis said. They could see longer wait times, he predicts, and even their private insurance could get more expensive to help subsidize care for people who no longer have coverage.</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health at WBEZ.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson on Jaguars' Liam Coen's shot at QB Caleb Williams: He can handle it
entries.summary: <p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>’ popularity skyrockets amid the expectation that he’s on the brink of joining the NFL’s elite passers, it’s not surprising that some in the league might already be getting tired of hearing about it.</p><p>Most notably, he’s on the cover of the forthcoming Madden 27 video game, a distinction that recently went to players who already had become All-Pros, MVPs and champions like Tom Brady, Patrick Mahomes, Lamar Jackson and Saquon Barkley.</p><p>The reality is that Williams isn’t in those guys’ class yet and is very much still a work in progress, something he and coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> have been saying for months. He led some incredible comebacks and delivered some incomparable throws; He also finished last in completion percentage and 22nd in passer rating.</p><p>That became a talking point 1,000 miles away at Jaguars training camp, where coach Liam Coen highlighted the contrast between the hype about Williams and the minimal attention his team gets.</p><p>“This is the best part of coaching the Jacksonville Jaguars: You don't have to make up [stuff to tell your players],” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/31/bears-caleb-williams-liam-coen-complain-attention-nfl-network-jaguars" >Coen said</a> on radio station 1010 XL. “You don’t have to make up the fire. It's given to us every day. It's a gift from the heavens.</p><p>“I just pull out my phone, look up the [NFL] website and I'm just curious if I see any photos or anything about the Jacksonville Jaguars. I'll see 40 pictures of Caleb Williams and I won't see a single thing about any of our players on here. It's beautiful … I'm just going to tell all these guys how much you all think they suck, and we'll just keep going."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">“All I’ll see is 40 pictures of Caleb Williams… and not a single thing about any of our players.” 😂<br><br>Liam Coen had a hilarious way of describing why he loves coaching the Jaguars on The Drill with Dan Hicken and Jeff Prosser.<br><br>🎥 WATCH NOW: <a href="https://t.co/E5etiiSE3n">https://t.co/E5etiiSE3n</a><a href="https://x.com/hashtag/DUUUVAL?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#DUUUVAL</a> |… <a href="https://t.co/idQZCvDMkK">pic.twitter.com/idQZCvDMkK</a></p>— 1010 XL / 92.5 FM (@1010XL) <a href="https://x.com/1010XL/status/2082949597261910044?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams, who revels in being ripped, reposted the widely viewed view clip of Coen’s comments on his X account.</p><p>Predictably, Johnson wasn’t in much of a mood to talk about it before practice Friday and quickly responded, “Well, we’re the No. 1 regression candidate. So we’ve got plenty of motivation ourselves.”</p><p>There’s no actual statistic for that, but many are skeptical about the Bears coming off a stunning 11-6 season built on improbable late escapes as they now face, on paper, the hardest schedule in the NFL. They’re 15th in odds to win the Super Bowl, behind NFC North rivals the Packers and Lions.</p><p>As for another coach tossing Williams’ name around, that’s another non-concern.</p><p>“He’s used to handling a lot of attention, so I’m not worried about that,” Johnson said.</p><p>The Bears host the Jaguars, who won the AFC South at 13-4 last season, in Week 13.</p>

The biggest among them was making the women's national team and playing professionally.</p><p>This Saturday, the 18-year-old will bat for the L.A. Queens as they face the New York Heights at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield for the Women’s Professional Baseball League’s opening day.</p><p>Hondras' loved ones already made the 100-mile trip from the south suburbs with a cardboard cutout of her face to cheer her on last weekend, and plan to continue through the WPBL season.</p><p>It's all taking place in Illinois — where women’s baseball flourished more than 70 years ago — as a new generation of professional players steps up.</p><p>"I don’t think it gets more full circle than that," Hondras told the Sun-Times. entries.title: Legisladores demócratas de Illinois y otros estados presionan para que ICE rinda cuentas a nivel nacional
entries.summary: <p>Un grupo de legisladores estatales demócratas de todo el país estuvo en Chicago el miércoles para impulsar más leyes que otorguen al público la posibilidad de demandar a agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) por tiroteos mortales y detenciones realizadas sin órdenes judiciales.</p><p>“Nunca imaginé que pasaría la mayor parte de mis dos primeros años en el cargo redactando leyes y apoyando normas que protejan a la gente de nuestro propio gobierno federal”, dijo la senadora estatal Graciela Guzmán, demócrata por Chicago, quien encabezó una conferencia de prensa organizada por un grupo de defensa conocido como State Innovation Exchange.</p><p>“Pensé que hablaríamos de reducir los costos de la atención médica, reducir gastos, financiar nuestras escuelas y luchar por un Illinois más equitativo. En cambio, esta administración ha obligado a estados como el nuestro a realizar otro tipo de trabajo, que es defender a nuestras comunidades del intervencionismo federal”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El otoño pasado, Illinois se convirtió en uno de los pocos estados del país en permitir que los residentes demanden a agentes de inmigración que violen sus derechos constitucionales al debido proceso y que los proteja contra registros e incautaciones irrazonables.</p><p>El proyecto de ley 1312 de la Cámara se convirtió en ley el otoño pasado. Otra disposición clave de la ley prohíbe las detenciones civiles relacionadas con inmigración en y alrededor de las cortes de Illinois.</p><p>Legisladores de otros estados, incluidos Georgia, Maryland, Utah, Colorado y Minnesota, dijeron que también están impulsando medidas de protección para sus residentes.</p><p>“Tenemos agentes federales que han roto ventanas de autos y han hecho llover cristales sobre niños de 1 año, o que han tirado al suelo a señoras que protestaban pacíficamente”, dijo el senador estatal de Colorado Mike Weissman. “Todos los que estamos aquí somos legisladores estatales que creemos profundamente en usar el poder que tenemos bajo nuestra constitución estatal para simplemente intentar hacer la vida de nuestros constituyentes más habitable y digna”.</p><p>Los homicidios por disparos de Renee Good y Alex Pretti en Minnesota en enero, y ahora el hecho de que se esté siguiendo a inmigrantes con visas vencidas en aeropuertos de Estados Unidos son ejemplos de por qué los legisladores estatales tienen que actuar con rapidez con legislación, dijo el senador estatal de Minnesota, Omar Fateh.</p><p>Fateh, cuyo distrito está en el lado sur de Minneapolis, dijo que presentó un proyecto de ley a principios de 2024 para proteger a los habitantes de Minnesota contra la violación de sus derechos por parte de agentes de inmigración. Pero dijo que sus compañeros legisladores consideraron que era demasiado pronto, demasiado arriesgado políticamente y demasiado hipotético para aprobarlo.</p><p>“A finales de 2025, Trump envió a Minnesota a 3,000 agentes armados, enmascarados y sin entrenamiento. Fue la mayor invasión federal en la historia estadounidense en un estado que tiene menos del 1% de la población indocumentada del país. Los agentes de Trump arrestaron a personas al azar en la calle, detuvieron a familias enteras, a niños pequeños, a madres y a ancianas”, dijo Fateh.</p><p>“Perseguían, acosaban, detenían, arrestaban y encarcelaban a habitantes de Minnesota en todas las etapas del proceso migratorio, incluidos quienes tenían estatus legal, refugiados, ciudadanos naturalizados, incluso ciudadanos de segunda y tercera generación, y luego mataron a dos observadores civiles, Renee Good y Alex Pretti”, añadió Fateh. “De repente, la lucha por proteger a la gente del fascismo de Trump pasó de ser prematura a parecer demasiado tarde”.</p><p>Guzmán, copresidenta del Caucus Legislativo Latino de Illinois, dijo que se han presentado cinco demandas bajo la nueva ley.</p><p><i>Michael Puente es reportero y presentador de WBEZ. Contáctalo en </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><i>mpuente@wbez.org</i></a><i>. </i><br><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: New Illinois law aims to rein in 'snake oil' social media apps getting kids hooked on scrolling
entries.summary: <p>TikTok, Snapchat, Instagram and other Big Tech giants will be required to strengthen privacy settings for minors under new Illinois legislation that seeks to crack down on addictive social media designs that keep kids scrolling for hours on end.</p><p>The Children’s Social Media Safety Act, signed into law Friday by Gov. JB Pritzker, takes aim at addictive algorithms that can glue young people to their phones to the detriment of their mental health.</p><p>“They feed our kids an unrealistic picture of life and sell them products and agendas to achieve it,” Pritzker said at a South Side bill signing. “The issue is they're selling snake oil — frankly, they're selling lies. When their business model depends on keeping kids' attention at any cost, their well-being takes a backseat. Today, Illinois is saying enough is enough.”</p><p>The legislation, which was passed unanimously by the Illinois General Assembly in the spring, puts guardrails around how companies can direct content to young people, rather than restrict the content itself.</p><p>Kids will still have access to the popular apps, but their feeds will be limited to accounts that they follow — not targeted content — with posts shared in chronological order. Their profiles won’t be accessible to adult strangers, with notifications blacked out from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.</p><p>“We're closing the door, and we will do everything within our power to make sure that the predators do not have access to the children within the state of Illinois,” said the bill's chief sponsor, state Sen. Willie Preston, D-Chicago. “Innovation and child safety are not competing interests. You do not have to choose between technological progress and protecting children.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a30000" name="image-a30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0017df6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/41db909/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/202ba50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Gov. JB Pritzker signs legislation in Chicago Friday targeting social media's potential harm to young people." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/202ba50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b677a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/202ba50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2846x1597+0+119/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fbb%2F0d5cd6cc42f2a509746564321c11%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-31-at-11-11-58-am.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gov. JB Pritzker signs legislation in Chicago Friday targeting social media’s potential harm to young people.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>State of Illinois livestream</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The companies have to establish an “age assurance system” that doesn’t require an ID or facial recognition.</p><p>Parents will set their child’s age while setting up the youngster’s device, which will signal apps to deploy the safeguards for minors. Parents will be able to tweak the settings under the law, which goes into effect Jan. 1, 2028.</p><p>The nonpartisan Taxpayers Protection Alliance opposed the legislation in Springfield, calling it “a step toward age verification and allowing the government to police speech.”</p><p>Pritzker’s office says the law’s focus on design features rather than content means “children can still access information and community online but aren’t subjected to the most harmful and addictive features of social media platforms.”</p><p>The law also shields minors’ locations and limits digital currency transactions, and their accounts won’t be visible to adult strangers or pop up on algorithmically curated “for you” pages.</p><p>News websites, broadband service providers, email providers and learning management systems are exempt from the requirements. Companies that don’t comply face $50,000 penalties for each violation.</p><p>Former U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy proposed putting warning labels on social media sites akin to those slapped on packs of cigarettes, citing studies that have shown harmful effects on mental health.</p><p>Chief House sponsor state Rep. Jennifer Gong-Gershowitz, D-Glenview, said the law “doesn't solve this problem on its own, but it says something important.</p><p>“The platforms have a responsibility to the children using them — that our kids deserve the chance to explore, make mistakes and grow up on their own terms, not on an algorithm’s,” she said. “That's what this bill is about, giving our children room to be children, free of a feed that's optimized to grab their attention, instead of encouraging their self-esteem, their well-being and their opportunity to grow.”</p>

entries.title: Sky coach Tyler Marsh says the 'film doesn't lie': Kamilla Cardoso deserves more free throws
entries.summary: <p>Tyler Marsh hadn't brought it up in a while, but you could tell he'd been sitting on it.</p><p>It’s been an undercurrent of frustration all season: The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> coach is convinced his leading scorer doesn't get enough foul calls. Watch the sideline when 6’7 center Kamilla Cardoso goes up and comes down empty-handed, and there's Marsh, chasing after officials.</p><p>Thursday night, the tide turned — at least momentarily. Cardoso shot a season-high 11 free throws in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/30/dijonai-carrington-jumps-back-in-and-helps-the-sky-finish" >Sky’s win over the Sun</a>, riding them to a game-high 26 points. It gave Marsh an opening to drive the point home.</p><p>"I can make a case that she should shoot close to 11 free throws every game," Marsh said. "I think she gets held a ton. I think that, for someone who shoots the majority of shots in the paint, there's just physically very little resistance that you can give without fouling her. She's just that forceful.</p><p>"To go games where she has zero to five free throws, it just doesn't make sense to me. And the film doesn't lie either."</p><p>Cardoso was the Sky's answer to righting the ship against the Sun. They stumbled through a lackluster first half, in part because foul trouble kept her on the bench for most of it. Once she returned, she took over: 18 points in the fourth quarter, with nine trips to the line.</p><p>"I don't remember the last time I shot a free throw," she joked afterward.</p><p>So why was this game different?</p><p>"Just me being aggressive, and the refs finally giving me the call," she said.</p><p>The numbers back at least part of the Sky’s argument. Cardoso shoots 4.1 free-throw attempts per game, just 20th in the league, despite taking 9.2 shots per game in the paint, eighth most.</p><p>Marsh has said throughout the season that the team regularly send clips of what they consider missed calls to the league office for review — and rarely hear back.</p><p>However, according to an Athletic report, the league did acknowledge missed calls in the Sky's fourth-quarter collapse against the Wings in late June. That included the whistle on Cardoso in the final minute that fouled her out and led to the Wings' go-ahead free throws.</p><p>Officiating has been a leaguewide pain point over the last two seasons. After sharp criticism from players and coaches last year, the WNBA created a task force of coaches and general managers to push for greater consistency, with an emphasis on calling illegal contact more tightly to protect freedom of movement.</p><p>Reviews have been mixed. Coaches generally concede that meaningful change takes time, but they still complain about too many consequential calls being missed. Next season, the league will add an off-site replay center designed to put more decisions in the hands of an objective third party. That's a significant investment that shows the league is serious.</p><p>In the meantime, the Sky have to live with the whistle they get.</p><p>And right now, a lot of it is blowing on Cardoso. The whistles Marsh wants on offense find her on the other end: she’s committing 3.6 fouls per game, third most in the league. Getting that number down will take better discipline and situational awareness from Cardoso.</p><p>Silly fouls — particularly the ones she picks up far from the basket — have been an issue since she entered the league.</p><p>The Sky can't afford them. Their offense now runs through Cardoso and isn't built to survive her sitting long stretches. Not every opponent will let her take over a fourth quarter — some, like the Aces on Saturday, are good enough to bury the Sky before she gets the chance.</p><p>The league needs to keep fixing its officiating, and Marsh should keep advocating for his star. Cardoso's job is to pick her battles, accept how the game is being called — and remember how badly the Sky need her on the floor.</p>

entries.title: Illinois panel rules cancer-stricken ex-cop convicted of murdering unarmed Black woman should stay in prison
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Prisoner Review Board Friday denied a bid from a cancer-stricken former downstate sheriff’s deputy convicted of murdering an unarmed Black woman to be released from prison early.</p><p>Sean Grayson, who is white, is serving a 20-year-sentence for fatally shooting Springfield area resident Sonya Massey in her kitchen two years ago. And despite a jury finding him guilty of second degree murder, Grayson maintained in his petition for early release that the 36-year-old Massey “attacked him with a pot of boiling water” when he responded to her 911 call.</p><p>Without commenting on its decision, the three-person panel made up of two Republicans and one Democrat voted unanimously against setting Grayson free after deliberating for just 10 minutes. Neither Grayson, his legal team nor supporters were present.</p><p>In a press conference following the hearing, Massey’s family and friends celebrated the decision.</p><p>“They did the right thing,” James Wilburn, Massey’s father, said. “[The board] did not perpetrate the serious miscarriage of justice. ”</p><p>In a statement after the panel's vote, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said Massey has left a lasting legacy on the state.</p><p>“Sonya Massey’s family and loved ones remain in my thoughts today. Her killing was a profound loss that can never be reversed. Sonya was innocent, unarmed, and calling law enforcement for help. It was a painful reminder that too many innocent Black Americans have faced this kind of violence — and they deserve justice," the governor said.</p><p>Grayson sought early release through the state’s Joe Coleman Medical Release Act, which allows those in custody who are terminally ill or who have a medical condition that incapacitates them to apply for early release from prison.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/fulltext?DocName=073000050K3-3-14" target="_blank" ><u>The law,</u></a> which was signed in 2022, spells out terminal illness as a condition that is irreversible, incurable and is likely to cause death within 18 months. According to his defense attorneys, Grayson is battling stage 4 colon cancer that has spread to his liver and lungs. He was first diagnosed in 2023.</p><p>In his petition, which was obtained by WBEZ, Grayson indicated his cancer is irreversible, incurable and will likely cause death within 18 months, though he is able to perform basic activities, like feeding and dressing himself.</p><p>The panel, which handles all traditional parole and clemency cases, reviewed a medical evaluation from the Illinois Department of Corrections. In addition, the board considered how much Grayson’s treatment would cost the state and how his incarceration would impact IDOC’s ability to provide medical care to others.</p><p>Grayson does have the option to re-apply as many times as he wants, an agency spokesperson said. His legal team declined a request for comment.</p><p>On July 6, 2024, Grayson and another officer responded to Massey’s call reporting a potential prowler. The interaction escalated in a matter of minutes, when Grayson threatened to “shoot [Massey] in the f– face” as he focused on a pot of boiling water on her stove. Body-worn camera footage shows an unarmed Massey ducking behind her kitchen counter as Grayson fired his duty weapon at her three times, striking her in the face.</p><p>During Grayson’s trial, prosecutors zeroed in on the shooting itself and the moments immediately following. Grayson can be seen refusing to administer first aid to Massey, telling his partner Massey had “a head shot, dude — she’s done,” and calling her a “crazy b–” when paramedics and other officers arrived at the scene.</p><p>Sangamon County State’s Attorney John Milhiser told the jury last fall Grayson’s actions were “out of bounds for civilized society.” In a letter to the Prisoner Review Board earlier this month, Milhiser urged the panel to deny Grayson’s release petition, saying the ex-cop was already diagnosed with cancer when he shot Massey.</p><p>“His temper and willingness to escalate minor misunderstandings into fatal encounters shows that he poses a danger… Cancer does not make him less dangerous,” Milhiser wrote.</p><p>Grayson also previously sought a reduced sentence in May, which a downstate judge swiftly denied.</p><p>A WBEZ open records request found no letters of support were submitted to the Prisoner Review Board on behalf of Grayson ahead of his hearing. However, four members of Massey’s family read victim impact statements before the panel.</p><p>Her mother, Donna Massey, told the board her daughter’s life was worth more than the several months that Grayson has spent in prison so far.</p><p>“Letting Sean Grayson out… for compassion? Where’s the compassion he gave to Sonya?” Massey said. “She was a young mother of two, and she got shot in her face for saying, ‘I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.’”</p>
entries.author: Mawa Iqbal | WBEZ

entries.title: Chicago police release videos of suspects sought in fatal South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police on Friday released video footage showing two suspects wanted in the deadly shooting of man who was found inside a car with a small child last year in South Shore.</p><p>Police are seeking to identify the two males suspected of shooting the 35-year-old man in the 2000 block of East 79th St. on June 7, 2025.</p><p>That evening, officers found the man slumped inside a vehicle with a gunshot wound to the right arm, police said. He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center and was later pronounced dead.</p><p>A 4-year-old boy who was also inside the car was unharmed, police said.</p><p>The suspects, both described as Black males, were captured on home-surveillance cameras before and after the shooting, police said.</p><p>One of the suspects is shown wearing a black and gray hooded sweater with a red shirt and dark pants, police said. The other was wearing a black hooded sweater and ripped jeans.</p><p>Anyone with information about the shooting should call Area Two Detectives at (312) 747-8271 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com, using the case number JJ285418.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/1tWGKGDJd4c?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Homicide | 7800 block of S. Clyde | June 7, 2025 | JJ285418"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Trabajadores de cementerio en suburbio de Chicago detenidos por ICE se suman a las demandas nacionales
entries.summary: <p>Dos trabajadores de un cementerio de los suburbios que fueron arrestados por agentes federales de inmigración el otoño pasado están demandando al gobierno federal como parte de un esfuerzo nacional de la Unión Estadounidense por las Libertades Civiles (ACLU) para responsabilizar a empleados del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>Los dos trabajadores, ambos ciudadanos estadounidenses, alegan que les rociaron con spray de pimienta y fueron arrestados indebidamente por agentes el pasado octubre mientras trabajaban en el Cementerio Concordia de Forest Park. Presentaron sus reclamaciones en marzo bajo la Ley Federal de Reclamaciones por Agravios, que permite a las personas solicitar una compensación económica por actos de mala conducta de empleados del gobierno federal.</p><p>Darren Eichler y Daniel Greer trabajaban en el terreno del cementerio cuando vieron a agentes de inmigración intentar arrestar a un hombre que estaba de pie en el Río Des Plaines, que corre junto al cementerio. Desde detrás de la reja del cementerio, Eichler, Greer y otros dos compañeros pidieron a los agentes que se retiraran del área y dejaran de acosar a la gente, según sus denuncias.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En lugar de eso, los agentes se acercaron y exigieron que los dejaran entrar al cementerio. Al negarse, los agentes sacaron un cortacadenas y cortaron el candado de la reja, según las denuncias. El agente los roció con gas pimienta y los arrestó.</p><p>Eichler empezó a sentir fuertes dolores en el pecho y dificultad para respirar. Pidió en varias ocasiones ser trasladado al hospital, pero los agentes tardaron más de una hora en llevarlo al Hospital Rush en Oak Park, donde lo mantuvieron esposado. Finalmente fue dado de alta del hospital sin cargos, según su demanda.</p><p>Mientras tanto, a Greer le rociaron con el spray, lo empujaron al suelo y le ataron las manos con bridas de plástico detrás de la espalda, según su demanda. Fue llevado a una instalación del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) pero nunca le explicaron por qué lo detuvieron ni le ofrecieron atención médica por las quemaduras químicas en el rostro.</p><p>También fue liberado sin cargos, pero le entregaron documentos que afirmaban que había sido arrestado por "agredir o resistirse a un oficial", según la demanda.</p><p>"A medida que los agentes intensificaban su ataque contra nosotros, no dejaba de pensar que se detendrían y reconocerían que su comportamiento no era correcto", dijo Greer en un comunicado de la ACLU. "En cada paso, aumentaron la violencia y nos trataron como basura".</p><p>DHS no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Los dos hombres se suman a otras 54 personas que han presentado demandas contra el gobierno federal. En el comunicado, ACLU dijo que lidera el esfuerzo para ayudar a "decenas de personas y familias que buscan justicia por el daño que sufrieron a manos de agentes federales de inmigración".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
