entries.title: Bears Training Camp Report: Practice No. 3
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> Friday training camp practice:</p><h3><b>What happened</b></h3><p>As good as the Bears were at two-minute drills toward the end of games, they struggled at the end of the first half. So coach Ben Johnson was curious what they’d do in the final drill Friday, when they practiced end-of-half offense.</p><p>In 1:22, quarterback Caleb Williams marched the Bears 61 yards, capping the drive with a 14-yard touchdown to tight end Colston Loveland with 15 seconds to play. It was an impressive bounce-back for Loveland, who dropped a touchdown earlier, and Williams, who'd been picked by Jaylon Johnson.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Best thing I saw at <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/Bears?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Bears</a> practice today was Colston Loveland’s TD catch in the two-minute drill. No photos for reporters so .. <a href="https://t.co/dsweAuJZC9">pic.twitter.com/dsweAuJZC9</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2083231045046939745?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Bears practiced in front of fans for the first time. A former player watched, too — three-time Pro Bowl offensive lineman Kyle Long, a new CBS pregame show co-host, sat in on Johnson’s press conference and signed autographs for fans during practice.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">These media guys are getting bigger every day. <a href="https://x.com/Ky1eLong?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Ky1eLong</a> <a href="https://t.co/3wjTWk1hc8">pic.twitter.com/3wjTWk1hc8</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2083172170717372645?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Position Battle Watch</h3><p>Kiran Amegadjie played first-team left tackle for the first time in camp, with Braxton Jones and Jedrick Wills splitting time with the second team. The Bears rotated left tackles in camp last year, too. Jones is still considered the favorite.</p><h3>Injury report</h3><p>Running back Kyle Monangai missed his second-straight practice. Everyone else who practiced Thursday participated Friday.</p><h3>What’s next</h3><p>The Bears practice at 8:30 a.m. Saturday.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Sun-Times free exhibition at Navy Pier of murals and other public art is newly updated
entries.summary: <p>Since the Chicago Sun-Times launched the weekly<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals" > “Murals and Mosaics”</a> series in July 2019, we're published at least one feature story on public art each week.</p><p>That's more than 360 stories, all of them devoted to spotlighting street art in the city and suburbs and the artists behind those works. And we've covered more in a weekly newsletter sent to subscribers and in special supplements.</p><p>We've also been highlighting that coverage with a public exhibition at Navy Pier, near our newsroom, displaying some of the many photographs of Chicago murals we've published. Now, we've added more images to that free display.</p><p>The exhibition opened in 2023. Among the newly added images, it now includes a photo of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals/2026/05/01/chicago-murals-roseland-footwork-antoine-humphries-twan-twan" target="_blank" >a two-story mural</a> in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/roseland" >Roseland</a> that focuses on Chicago’s “footwork culture.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Amid contract talks, Bears RT Darnell Wright knows he'll 'be here for a long time'
entries.summary: <p> Just Tuesday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> general manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/27/bears-ben-johnson-ryan-poles-training-camp-four-questions-caleb-williams-braxton-jones-kyler-gordon-dayo-odeyingbo-nfl" target="_blank" >Ryan Poles</a> made it sound as if he wasn’t close to a contract extension for right tackle Darnell Wright.</p><p>Friday, though, Wright was clear — he plans to stay with the Bears for years to come.</p><p>“I know I'll be here for a long time,” he said. “Hopefully my whole career."</p><p>Wright is entering the fourth year of his rookie deal, though the Bears have already picked up his rookie option in 2027. Given that the option will pay about $19 million, the Bears are motivated to find a rich, but more salary cap-friendly, extension.</p><p>The Bears figure to make Wright one of the highest-paid players at his position. Earlier this week, the Vikings gave their right tackle, Brian O’Neill, a four-year, $96 million <br>deal with $66.7 guaranteed.</p><p>Tuesday, Poles stressed that he wanted to keep the former first-rounder.</p><p>“There’s a window to get a deal done and then at some point we’ve got to go play football,” Poles said. “So we’ll figure that part out. But obviously — I think I’ve said it before — Darnell’s a guy we want here long-term.”</p><p>That window figures to close when the Bears open against the Panthers on Sept. 13. In the past, Poles has cut extensions for Cole Kmet and DJ Moore during training camp.<br></p>

Seeing the two join forces on the track and end with a sincere embrace was symbolic of the whole Lollapalooza weekend. </p><p>With a bill dominated by women artists, the collab was the ultimate display of girl power and set the standard for all the other unexpected bits to come over the weekend.</p><p>For Lorde, it was also one more way to help “complete the circle” of her Lolla journey that began in 2014 when she was just 17. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lorde performs in the rain on day one of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Thursday, Aug. 3, 2017. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lorde slipped in abbreviated takes of the songs she knew she had to, like “Royals,” to allow time for the other material she wanted to really focus on, particularly from her latest album “Virgin.” The record is a stark body of work about bodily autonomy and personal rebirth, and Lorde laid herself bare on songs like “Broken Glass” (about an eating disorder), pairing it with a set that was just as raw and stripped back. </p><p>She also went "way back” with early cuts like “Buzzcut Season” and “Ribs.” And she also had the opportunity to finally do “The Louvre,” the song she was apparently “most looking forward” to performing at Lolla in 2017 before the weather interrupted.</p><p>Beyond the well-curated set list, at the heart of the performance was a rumination on humanity trapped in a world that seems to keep wanting to sterilize existence. The New Zealander started the 20-song suite hooked up to machines that were monitoring her vitals while video screens took a bird’s eye view of the dizzying amount of electronics on the stage that produced the night’s synth explosion. Symbolically, though, the juxtaposition felt like the ultimate clash of people vs. robots. </p><p>Lorde has often talked about her disdain for AI — taking Meta Glasses and Spotify to task in recent diatribes — and she opened up on her stance in her Lolla set, too.</p><p>“The future looks a little bit different than I imagined. It’s harder and darker. I dream about fire all the time now, and I’m scared. But us meeting up and dancing and crying and singing to each other, that is one of the best ways I have to feel alive,” she told the crowd. “I’m sorry to say it’s going to get harder and darker, but we can stay awake, we can stay alive . . . I want you to ask yourself every day, am I acting trapped or do I wish I could be acting free?”</p><p>The speech was part necessity — Lorde was trying to buy time and give security a chance to attend to fans in the crowd who kept passing out from a combination of the day’s high temps and the wall of bodies that were pressed up near the stage. </p><p>But it also felt right on cue as a takeaway for caring about each other in these dire times. “We gotta stay awake in this moment . . . it’s ours and it’s beautiful,” she added. “And I promise I’ll keep singing to you through all of it.”</p><div entries.title: Escuelas secundarias latinas podrían ser las más afectadas por recortes de maestros en el presupuesto de CPS
entries.summary: <p>A la maestra veterana Anna Acosta le dan escalofríos al pensar cómo reaccionarán los alumnos de la Secundaria Kelly cuando lleguen el próximo mes y descubran que una decana muy querida ya no está.</p><p>Sospecha que el despido de la decana afectará especialmente a los estudiantes inmigrantes que recientemente han sido parte de la escuela y que acudían a ella en busca de apoyo.</p><p>“Ella fue extremadamente, extremadamente útil para tender puentes y también para reparar daños, y era muy respetada”, dijo Acosta, que imparte historia en la secundaria del vecindario de Brighton Park, en el suroeste de la ciudad. “Estoy segura de que mis alumnos van a decir ‘¿Dónde está la señorita Montoya? La queríamos’”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-320000" name="module-320000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Y no se trata solo de una decana. Kelly también perdió cinco puestos de maestros, además de dos puestos de especialistas en intervención que ayudaban a los estudiantes con dificultades. El resultado: se ofrecerán menos clases y las que queden tendrán más alumnos.</p><p>Secundarias como la Kelly están sufriendo con fuerza los recortes presupuestarios que los funcionarios del distrito reconocen que afectarán la experiencia estudiantil. Al presentar el presupuesto a principios de este mes, el distrito dijo que recortará cerca de 1,000 puestos de enseñanza básicos, que incluyen maestros de inglés y matemáticas, así como maestros de arte.</p><p>Pero el lunes, las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) solo divulgaron públicamente información sobre cómo exactamente los recortes afectan a cada escuela, apenas días antes de la votación presupuestaria del jueves y semanas más tarde de lo habitual.</p><p>Un análisis de WBEZ sobre los cambios presupuestarios a nivel escolar muestra que las secundarias con mayoría de estudiantes latinos estarían perdiendo la mayor cantidad de maestros, tanto en proporción de su plantilla como en número absoluto. Perdieron 158 maestros, es decir, el 7% de su personal docente.</p><p>En general, hay alrededor del 4% menos de maestros en todas las escuelas, sin contar a los que trabajan específicamente con estudiantes de educación especial. WBEZ analizó las pérdidas de maestros según el tipo de escuela y la demografía estudiantil.</p><p>La superintendente Macquline King calificó el presupuesto de desafiante y, como exdirectora, dijo que le resulta difícil saber que estos recortes afectan a los estudiantes. Pero señaló que los directores, junto con sus consejos escolares locales (LSCs), toman muchas de las decisiones sobre a quién despedir y a quién mantener.</p><p>“Esas escuelas y esas comunidades saben qué necesitan más sus niños y confiamos en que ellas informen sobre esos presupuestos”, comentó.</p><p>Hay dos razones coincidentes por las que las secundarias latinas sufrieron los recortes más profundos. Para cerrar un enorme déficit presupuestario, el distrito escolar aumentó el número de estudiantes que cada maestro puede atender. Al mismo tiempo, muchas escuelas secundarias predominantemente latinas han visto disminuir sus inscripciones.</p><p>Las inscripciones de Kelly bajaron en alrededor de 100 alumnos el último año escolar.</p><p>Norma Ríos Sierra, miembro de la junta escolar que representa el noroeste de la ciudad, dijo que ha escuchado a directores de su zona que intentan cuadrar los presupuestos con los recortes. La única escuela secundaria del vecindario de su distrito, Roosevelt, ha perdido ocho puestos docentes, según datos de CPS.</p><p>Destacó que esas pérdidas se deben a la disminución en las inscripciones y a un esfuerzo del distrito por asegurar un financiamiento equitativo. Cuando el distrito tiene recursos limitados, termina enfrentando unas escuelas contra otras, señaló.</p><p>Le preocupa que cada pérdida de personal sea perjudicial y que la presión sobre las escuelas “se traslade a la experiencia de los estudiantes”.</p><p>La información a nivel escolar también revela que otros programas y personal que no se abordaron en las presentaciones presupuestarias iniciales están siendo recortados. Hay la mitad del dinero para pagar al personal u organizaciones que implementen planes de seguridad escolar.</p><p>Cuarenta escuelas perdieron asistentes escolares que, como en Kelly, a menudo cumplen el papel de decanos, mientras que dos docenas de escuelas perdieron a su coordinador tecnológico.</p><p>Una directora de una secundaria del noroeste dijo que su escuela de más de 1,000 alumnos ahora solo cuenta con un puesto de coordinador tecnológico a medio tiempo. Agregó que tuvo que eliminar a su coordinador tecnológico a tiempo completo junto con seis puestos más. No quiso ser identificada porque CPS no le dio permiso para ser entrevistada.</p><p>Ella y su personal tenían grandes planes para el próximo año escolar, comentó, pero los recortes propuestos “les quitaron el impulso”.</p><p>Muchas escuelas están recibiendo menos fondos discrecionales de los que los directores suelen usar para pagar programas extracurriculares u otro personal, como monitores de cafeterías.</p><p>Y más escuelas están teniendo que usar fondos discrecionales para pagar a docentes o subdirectores, lo que también le quita dinero a otros programas.</p><p>Kia Banks, presidenta de la Asociación de Directores y Administradores de Chicago, dijo que no está bien obligar a los directores a usar sus limitados fondos discrecionales para cubrir puestos que debería cubrir el distrito. Quedó sorprendida en primavera cuando el distrito anunció que ya no cubriría los puestos de subdirectores en las escuelas con menos estudiantes inscritos.</p><p>Banks señala que la mayoría de los subdirectores desplazados son mujeres afroamericanas que trabajan en escuelas del sur y oeste. Dijo que el sindicato aún está negociando con el distrito para intentar recuperar esos puestos. No consideraba que la junta escolar deba aprobar el presupuesto tal como está el jueves porque carece de “el personal y los servicios que nuestros estudiantes necesitan”.</p><p>WBEZ no analizó los cambios a nivel escolar en maestros o asistentes de educación especial. CPS presupuestó más personal de educación especial este año que el año pasado. Sin embargo, el distrito incorpora personal de educación especial a medida que avanza el año escolar y ahora hay más estudiantes identificados con discapacidades, así como estudiantes con necesidades crecientes.</p><p>Este verano, CPS despidió o eliminó vacantes de aproximadamente 1,800 puestos de educación especial, pero muchos de esos puestos se volverán a incorporar a medida que avance el año escolar.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Man dead, woman injured in North Lawndale drive-by, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was killed and a woman was wounded in a drive-by shooting Friday afternoon in North Lawndale, police said.</p><p>The man, 27, standing near the street in the 3400 block of West 16th Street around 12:40 p.m. when he was approached by two vehicles and people inside started shooting, Chicago police said in a statement.</p><p>The man was struck multiple times, and a 56-year-old woman standing nearby was shot twice in her back, police said.</p><p>The pair was taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital, where the man was pronounced dead and the woman was listed in fair condition, police said. Additional details were not released.</p>

entries.title: CBS puts Tony Romo on leave after arrest on suspicion of operating vehicle under the influence
entries.summary: <p>Tony Romo has been placed on leave from his role as the lead analyst on CBS' NFL coverage following his arrest last week on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence.</p><p>CBS Sports announced Friday that the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback was on leave "until further notice." JJ Watt will join Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson as CBS Sports' lead NFL team during Romo's absence.</p><p>Romo, 46, was<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/07/24/tony-romo-arrested-on-suspicion-of-operating-a-vehicle-while-under-the-influence" > arrested July 23</a> after he was stopped while driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office report, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting taken into custody, booked and released.</p><p>He has a court date set for Sept. 21.</p><p>CBS Sports' announcement comes after citations released by the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office indicated an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found in the passenger's side of Romo's black Jeep during an inventory before it was towed.</p><p>According to the citations, police stopped Romo after he was seen passing cars in a gore area, which separates interstate traffic from cars entering from an on-ramp. Police said Romo questioned what a gore area was during the stop.</p><p>Body camera footage released earlier this week showed Romo telling deputies he had been coming from a golf course and was on his way "to visit grandma and grandpa" when he was stopped. A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had "red glassy eyes" and an "odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage."</p><p>Romo went to high school about 35 miles from Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.</p><p>He has been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during an NFL career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.</p><p>Romo remains the Cowboys' franchise leader in career touchdown passes with 248. He held the franchise record for career passing yards (34,183) until Dak Prescott overtook him last season.</p><p>Watt joined CBS in 2023. He was an analyst on "The NFL Today" for two seasons before teaming with Ian Eagle on the network's No. 2 crew beginning last season.</p><p>Romo wasn't expected to have his first game until the opening Sunday of the regular season on Sept. 13. CBS will air a preseason game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 28.</p><p>CBS likely will reveal its game assignments and announcer pairings for the first three weeks of the regular season in the next couple of weeks.<br></p>

entries.title: Heavy rain expected at Lollapalooza. Here’s what to know.
entries.summary: <p>Lollapalooza attendees may want to keep a poncho handy Friday afternoon, with forecasters expecting showers to move into downtown Chicago during the festival's second day.</p><p>Rain is expected to reach the downtown Chicago area between 1 and 2 p.m. Friday, with scattered showers developing through the afternoon before becoming more widespread and heavier during the evening and overnight, the National Weather Service said Friday morning.</p><p>"Everybody is going to get rain and most likely see rain amounts around and upward of an inch before all is said and done," said Zachary Yack, a meteorologist with the weather service.</p><p>Yack said Downtown is forecast to receive about 1 to 1.5 inches of rain, though localized areas could receive more than 2 inches, depending on where the heaviest rain develops.</p><p>The uncertainty, he said, is whether those highest rainfall totals fall over the city’s Downtown area or elsewhere. Yack said it looks like the heaviest, most steady rainfall will be happening after 5 to 6 p.m.</p><p>With the anticipated rainfall, ponding and localized flooding cannot be ruled out, particularly in low-lying areas, Yack said.</p><p>He added that festival grounds at Lollapalooza will likely become muddy, while lightning is expected to remain a relatively low threat, with about a 15% to 20% chance depending on location.</p><p>Here's what you need to know for Day 2.</p><h3><b>How will attendees know if weather changes disrupt the festival?</b></h3><p>Attendees are encouraged to check the festival website for updates, follow Lollapalooza on X, Facebook and Instagram, and opt in to push notifications through the Lolla mobile app, <a class="Link" href="https://www.festiverse.com/" target="_blank" >Festiverse</a>. Organizers said push notifications will include updates on the festival’s status, including any adjusted set times.</p><h3><b>What happens if Lollapalooza is evacuated?</b></h3><p>Lollapalooza’s website states that an evacuation does not necessarily mean the festival is canceled.</p><p>If Grant Park must be evacuated, attendees are directed to three underground parking garages: Grant Park North Garage at 25 N. Michigan Ave., Grant Park South Garage at 325 S. Michigan Ave. and Millennium Lakeside Garage at 5 S. Columbus Drive.</p><p>If attendees are allowed to reenter Grant Park following an evacuation, updated performance schedules will be available in the Lolla app, on the website's schedule page and on the festival's social media channels.</p><p>Once back inside the park, attendees can also check the video information tower near Buckingham Fountain for updated set times.</p><h3><b>What should festivalgoers bring — or leave at home?</b></h3><p>Lollapalooza festival organizers encourage attendees to dress for the weather by wearing rain-friendly shoes or boots and ponchos.</p><p>Umbrellas and towels are not allowed into the festival grounds, so music fans who don’t have a poncho can purchase one at the Lolla Bodega, according to the website.</p><p>Sunscreen is allowed only in non-aerosol containers of 3.4 ounces or less.</p><h3><b>Will the weather affect getting to and from Lollapalooza?</b></h3><p>The rainfall is expected after the majority of attendees will have arrived, with the festival gates opening at 11 a.m., though getting home could be more tedious.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Transportation shared on its social media channels that free Divvy valet parking will be available at the Millennium Park station at Michigan Avenue and Monroe Street through Sunday.</p><p>The Chicago Transit Authority and Metra have added service and capacity to existing train routes to serve the thousands of fans commuting to the four-day event, according to a Metra statement.</p><p>Through Sunday, Metra is running extra trains on seven of its 11 lines and adding railcars for expanded capacity to accommodate the drastic ridership boost.</p><p>CTA customers are encouraged to use the Red and Blue lines, and elevated lines in the Loop, to get to and from the festival. </p><p>Yellow Line service will be extended until 1 a.m. each night, and multiple bus routes will connect to Metra trains at Chicago Union Station or Ogilvie Transportation Center with Grant Park.</p><p>"CTA is prepared for all anticipated weather conditions, and CTA operations and maintenance personnel are deployed across the system throughout the day and through post-event to monitor conditions and minimize any weather-related impacts should they arise," a CTA spokesperson said in a statement. </p><p>Buses serving those routes will also have signs in their windows indicating they serve Lollapalooza, according to Metra.</p><p>Customers should keep an eye out for planned bus reroutes in the area due to festival-related street closures, CTA said.</p><p>The transit authority urged customers to visit CTA’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.transitchicago.com/lollapalooza/" target="_blank" ><u>Lollapalooza travel page</u></a> for festival-specific travel information.</p><p>“Over the past two decades, public transportation has been the most affordable and convenient way to travel to Lollapalooza,” said Metra CEO Jim Derwinski in a statement. “Metra and CTA are again working together to make the trip as easy as possible with added service as well as Day and Weekend Passes that make public transit the easiest choice to get to the festival.”</p><h3><b>Has this happened before?</b></h3><p>Yes, rain has fallen on festivalgoers multiple times, sometimes leading to evacuations.</p><p>In 2017, Lollapalooza organizers evacuated Grant Park around 9 p.m. on Day 1 of the music festival due to storms as Lorde and Muse were performing their headlining sets.</p><p>The music festival was temporarily suspended in 2012, with thousands of fans evacuated to shelters on a Saturday as the city faced storms with high winds. The festival was closed for about three hours.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-120000" name="module-120000"></a> <div entries.title: Illinois Institute of Technology cuts 160 faculty and staff just before fall semester
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Institute of Technology has laid off approximately 160 faculty and staff just before the start of the fall semester, a university spokesperson said in a written statement.</p><p>According to an email shared with WBEZ, the university’s president said Illinois Tech is facing research funding cuts and “severe restrictions on international students.”</p><p>“The university has no choice but to pursue targeted reductions to address these challenges and protect our mission as an opportunity engine for all,” Illinois Tech President Raj Echambadi wrote in an email to employees on Tuesday.</p><p>Illinois Tech, which has its main campus in Bronzeville and a law center downtown, is not the only university with these struggles. The Trump administration has significantly cut federal funding for university research and tightened regulations on foreign students.</p><p>The changes have discouraged and even disallowed international students from coming to the United States, which is hurting college finances. Foreign students typically pay higher tuition than domestic students.</p><p>The university reported that <a class="Link" href="https://www.iit.edu/oii/facts-and-reports" target="_blank" ><u>more than 40%</u></a> of students were from countries outside the U.S. in fall 2025. Six in 10 graduate students at the school were foreign.</p><p>Enrollment data posted on archives of Illinois Tech's website show a loss of approximately 1,200 international graduate students between the fall of 2024 and 2025 — a significant decline for a school that enrolled 7,500 students overall last year.</p><p>An Illinois Tech spokesperson did not detail how many faculty and staff have been laid off in each department. But several educators at the school said the cuts were deep and compounded by months of attrition following rumors of financial instability.</p><p>The university spokesperson said leaders recognize the changes “have a significant impact” on laid-off employees and are “committed to providing impacted colleagues with severance.”</p><p>“As always, we will continue to place students at the center of all that we do and to ensure educational excellence at Illinois Tech,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.</p><p>The university’s faculty senate issued a vote of no confidence in the president and provost on Monday, the day before faculty and staff began receiving layoff notices. In a letter to the university’s attorney shared with WBEZ, senate members acknowledged the campus is facing “extreme” financial difficulties but criticized how senior officials have handled them.</p><p>“The faculty do not trust the current senior administration to make the necessary decisions to navigate this transition in a way that meets our responsibilities to students and accreditors,” wrote Daniel Bliss, political science professor and faculty senate chair. “The current senior administration’s slow, opaque, apparently uninformed and non-transparent addressing of the crisis has deepened and aggravated its scope.”</p><p>Multiple employees said campus leadership have yet to communicate with students about the layoffs. The fall semester starts for much of the campus on Aug. 17.</p><p>“Students are concerned that we're going to be closed in two years, three years,” said one staffer who asked to remain anonymous because they fear retaliation from university administration. “They're worried they're not going to get the courses that they need because we don't have the faculty to teach them.”</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ, in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p>
entries.author: Lisa Kurian Philip | WBEZ

entries.title: 3 people found dead in Chicago Lawn apartment, police say
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are investigating the deaths of three people found inside a Chicago Lawn home Friday morning.</p><p>Officers were called to assist paramedics at an apartment in the 3300 block of West Marquette Road around 11 a.m., police said in a statement.</p><p>Inside, two males and a female, whose ages weren't shared, were found unresponsive, police said.. They were pronounced dead at the scene, police said. Their names have not been released. </p><p>It was not immediately known how long the people had been dead. Police said they were conducting a death investigation.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>
entries.author: Elijah James

entries.title: How one influencer navigated the TikTok to IRL pipeline at this year’s Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>Watching Elizabeth Nichols’ Lollapalooza debut on the BMI stage Thursday, you could see her win over the crowd in real time.</p><p>A smattering of diehard fans filmed videos while passionately singing along to her viral song, “I Got a New One.” But much of the crowd – waiting to see rising pop singer Bella Kay – was treated for the first time to Nichols’ short, cheeky songs about boys, religion and small-town gossip.</p><p>And they were charmed.</p><p>“I thought it was great,” said Gabrielle Seminaro, 23, of Hawthorn Woods. “She had a cute little vibe.”</p><p>Annmarie Johnson and her 13-year-old daughter, Taylor, complimented Nichols’ humor and storytelling.</p><p>“She’s like a young Taylor Swift,” said Johnson, 47, of Idaho.</p><div class="Enhancement" In the past few years, the platform has grown as a marketing tool for popular and unknown artists, and it shows no signs of losing steam. Whether it’s headliner Oliva Dean’s “Man I Need,” Bella Kay’s “iloveitiloveitiloveit,” Zara Larsson’s “Midnight Sun” or Illinois native Stella Lefty’s “Boston,” viral singles have captured the attention of this year’s festivalgoers.</p><p>But audiences are not content with hearing a trending tune. expecting any to gain widespread attention. But in 2024, “I Got a New One,” a clever song about replacing problematic love interests, took off. Fans made their own videos featuring the track, and Kelly Clarkson even performed a rendition on her talk show.</p><p>Nichols, whose videos gain millions of views, said she owes her success to social media.</p><p>“It is so awesome that it is free, and anybody can do it,” said Nichols, who dropped out of law school last year<b> </b>to focus on music full time. “Music is the most accessible it's ever been. I'm very blessed.”</p><p>By writing songs that are typically under three minutes, Nichols is following the popular trend of targeting young social media users with short attention spans. With just one EP, “Tough Love,” under her belt, Nichols is currently working on a full-length album. However, she consistently releases singles, including the forthcoming “Does Your Girlfriend Know We Kissed?,” her third this year. She debuted the track at Lollapalooza.</p><p>She also teases works in progress, including a clip from the viral “<a class="Link" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@elizabethnichols/video/7562329241828871479" target="_blank" ><u>Might Go Maga</u></a>” song that she posted in October. It is, ostensibly, about women betraying their morals to date Trump supporters, but Nichols wants listeners to draw their own conclusions.</p><p>“It's so fun watching people react and understand – or Bunny ears signaled fans of <b>Slayyyter,</b> the rising Missouri-born pop star, in the mix. Other artists on the day's schedule include 'Stranger Things' star <b>Finn Wolfhard</b>; the Swedish singer-songwriter <b>Zara Larsson</b>; and the enigmatic <b>Horsegiirl</b>, the German DJ known for entries.title: Cubs' Justin Steele says recovery is progressing, but no timetable for his return
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> left-hander Justin Steele said he is making progress in his recovery from an injury to his pitching elbow that has sidelined him for more than a year, though he has no target date for his return.</p><p>Steele would love nothing more than to be back, though he is also mindful of the setback he suffered rehabbing in April.</p><p>“Obviously, I want to be back,” he said. “Front office, the pitching coaches, the team — everybody wants me back. But you don’t want to rush it to the point where you do get back into games and you’re one or two outings in and you start to feel the soreness starting to creep back in and then you’re kind of turn the clock back at that point.”</p><p>Steele said he is pain-free. He has been rehabbing at the team’s facility in Mesa, Arizona, and in Chicago during homestands. He played catch on Friday and plans to throw about 20 pitches off the mound on Saturday.</p><p>“Everything feels good,” he said. “Fastball, sinker, slider, curveball — everything's there.”</p><p>An All-Star in 2023, Steele hasn’t pitched since he went seven innings in a win over Texas on April 7, 2025. He had season-ending surgery to repair the ulnar collateral ligament in his left elbow and appeared on track to return to the rotation perhaps in the first half this season. That changed when he suffered a flexor strain in late April, another blow for a pitching staff that’s been hit hard by injuries this season.</p><p>“He’s just starting to touch the mound,” manager Craig Counsell said. “He’s making progress. Everything’s going well.”</p><p>In other injury news, Counsell hoped Matt Shaw (sprained left hand) would hit Friday in Arizona. He said closer Daniel Palencia (right elbow inflammation) is scheduled to throw live batting practice on Saturday and will go on a rehab assignment before he returns from an injury that has kept him out since mid-June.</p><p>“There’s questions on Justin, still, because it’s been such a long time,” Counsell said. “Daniel’s coming back. He’s on his way back.”</p><p>The Cubs placed righty Gavin Hollowell on the 15-day injured list because of right-shoulder inflammation and recalled lefty Antoine Kelly from Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>The 26-year-old Kelly, a Maine Township East product, was acquired by the Cubs from the Los Angeles Dodgers in June. He previously pitched in Milwaukee’s system when Counsell managed the Brewers.</p><p>“He’s a talented arm,” Counsell said. “Throwing strikes has always been the key for Antoine. Some guys, it just takes a while for that to click. It’s gotten better in Iowa. … I’m so happy for a kid that’s had a pretty good journey in the minor leagues. A Chicago kid. I’m happy to be able to make his debut here.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Bears confidence in Johnson's 2nd year rooted in 3 words: 'We have Ben'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> assistants don’t typically spend a lot of time with coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/31/bears-coach-ben-johnson-on-jaguars-liam-coens-shot-at-qb-caleb-williams-he-can-handle-it" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> on game day.</p><p>That’s by design — Johnson is notoriously intense and not particularly chatty hours before kickoff — but also practical. Many of the team’s assistants head up to the coaching booth before Johnson’s pregame speech.</p><p>Even from the coaching box, though, they can <i>feel</i>  Johnson when he takes the field. His confidence is contagious, even through binoculars.</p><p>“Why do you think you're going to win?” offensive coordinator Press Taylor asked. “We have Ben. Like, that's a big part of it.”</p><p>Many around Halas Hall believe the same — that Johnson has the intoxicating blend of coaching acumen and force of personality the Bears have been missing since Mike Ditka was fired after the 1992 season.</p><p>His second season will be a test of just how right they are.</p><p>Spend enough time at Halas Hall — this is my 14<sup>th</sup> season — and you’re training to look for traps. <i>Marc Trestman often addressed the team from the back of the meeting room? John Fox wasn’t sure the Bears were going to draft Mitch Trubisky until the very end? Matt Nagy is going to keep using Cody Parkey even after all his regular-season misses? Matt Eberflus’ whole coaching ethos is rooted in a defensive film grading system?</i></p><p>Caution about Johnson’s second season, then, is essential. But his second training camp already feels more stable than the last time the Bears defended their NFC North crown.</p><p>In the offseason after the infamous “Double-Doink,” Nagy, the NFL Coach of the Year, held a kicking derby in which he believed that quiet — “Augusta Silence,” he called it — applied more pressure than crowd noise. It was a circus. Days later, the Bears held a convention in which many of their past heroes declared Nagy's team Super Bowl contenders. It was far too presumptuous for a team that didn’t even win a playoff game.</p><p>The Bears and Packers played in the NFL’s Thursday night opener. Nagy wore George Halas’ fedora into the stadium to commemorate the Bears’ 100<sup>th</sup> season. The Bears lost 10-3 and Trubisky had a 62.1 passer rating. </p><p>That momentum was lost forever.</p><p>Seizing it this year matters.</p><p>Cynicism is well-earned around these parts. Squint hard enough, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-caleb-williams-madden-27-cover-revealed-quarterback-video-game-nfl-ea-sports" >Caleb Williams’ “Madden” coronation</a> in June looks a bit like the Bears’ 2019 convention. Still, this training camp feels different — in part because Johnson feels the same. For all the attention received got in Year 1, from chanting “Good, Better, Best” to ripping off his shirt on “Black Friday” to filming a scene in an upcoming Hallmark movie, Johnson remains the same hard-driving head coach.</p><p>“I think that's the biggest compliment you can have,” receiver Rome Odunze said.</p><p>His demands haven’t changed. The players have noticed.</p><p>“I feel like the culture has been set,” defensive tackle Grady Jarrett said. “I feel like the expectations have been set.”</p><p>Those have been communicated — shouted, really — to his quarterback. After initially wondering if Johnson hated him, Williams has reacted to the daily challenges the way those at Halas Hall hoped he would.</p><p>“They both want to be great and win Super Bowls,” general manager Ryan Poles said. “That's all that matters.”</p><p>With a strong season, Johnson has a chance to define the Bears’ identity for the next decade: unflinchingly intense — remember him reaching full boil when a phone rang during his press conference? — with offensive panache. A we-do-what-want rushing attack with a takeaway-happy defense. A head coach stomping on the field and making those around him giddy he’s headed for their sideline.</p><p>“There were things when I took the job that I really strongly believed in — and so that's still going to be the pillars of it,” Johnson said Friday. “I don't want to deviate too far from things I believe in. I think we had some success and it worked. …</p><p>“It's really more about trusting the people around me, delegating, knowing their strengths and weaknesses better than I did before.”</p><p>That’s what Nagy didn’t have. Shortly after the “Double-Doink,” defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, Nagys best assistant, left to become the Broncos head coach. He look linebackers coach Brandon Staley, who went on to become the Chargers’ head coach, and defensive backs coach Ed Donatell with him.</p><p>Johnson, by contrast, returns almost all of his staff — all but offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, who didn’t call plays, and running backs coach Eric Bieniemy. Every day, Johnson said, he learns “a gold nugget” from defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, a two-time head coach.</p><p>In team meetings, Johnson and his coaches make it clear to their players the Bears have gone from being the hunter to being hunted. Coming off their first NFC North title since 2018, the Bears have the most difficult strength of schedule in the NFL. They have the weight of expectations, too, that have crushed previous Bears coaches.</p><p>If the was a secret to the Bears’ success last year, he said, it was the relationships formed in the summer.</p><p>“We're in a race right now to develop the same chemistry that we had a year ago," he said.</p><p>There will be some changes to training camp. The Bears purchased high-end cameras that allow them to cut up practice film in real time. Practice times will fluctuate in August, a nod to the short weeks and prime-time showings they’ll have to deal with all season. The grueling practice that molded the Bears last season? They’ll have another one of those soon.</p><p>Joint practices in Cincinnati and Nashville — and the hotel stays, meals and camaraderie that comes with them — were scheduled with the sole purpose of bonding the Bears.</p><p>What Johnson wants will remain the same.</p><p>“It’s going to be a physical, it’s going to be tough, it’s going to be a demanding ordeal,” Johnson said. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging. These guys all know that. entries.title: Sky could lose forward Chloe Bibby to the Lynx
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> suddenly have a hole in their frontcourt — and now they might lose one of the players patching it.</p><p>Starting forward Azura Stevens has been away from the team for the past week for personal reasons and will miss another game Saturday against the Aces. Meanwhile, the Lynx are attempting to poach one of her backups. </p><p>According to ESPN's Alexa Philippou, Minnesota has offered development player Chloe Bibby a standard contract. The Sky have until 4 p.m. CDT Saturday to promote Bibby to a standard contract of their own or lose her.</p><p>That's easier said than done. With no room under the salary cap, according to HerHoopStats, the Sky would need to cut or trade a player to make the move.</p><p>Bibby, a 6-2 stretch big, scored eight points with two assists off the bench in Thursday's win over the Sun. She also posted a career-high 14 points in a win over Seattle earlier this month. She has contributed to two wins in limited action — tough spare that with Stevens out.</p><p>Their only other active forwards are rookie Aicha Coulibaly, who started in Stevens' place Thursday, and development player Maddy Westbeld, whom the team has been reluctant to use.</p><p>This was a guard-heavy roster to begin with, and Rickea Jackson's season-ending knee injury stretched it thinner. Until Stevens returns, the Sky may need Natasha Cloud, their versatile guard, to spot minutes in the post.</p><p>They can also look to sign another forward to a development contract to replace entries.title: 2 hurt in West Garfield Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>Two men were wounded, one of them critically, in a shooting Friday in the West Garfield Park neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>The men, ages 30 and 36, were standing on the sidewalk in the 4400 block of West Monroe Street around 4:25 p.m. when four people exited a white sedan and opened fire, police said in a statement.</p><p>The younger man was shot in his thigh and calf and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in fair condition, police said. The older man suffered eight gunshot wounds and took himself to the same hospital, where he was listed in critical condition.</p><p>Police said the shooters were last seen driving west on Monroe.</p>

entries.title: Watchdog's report on Benton raises more questions about Speaker Welch's handling of sexual harassment
entries.summary: <p>It only takes “a cursory reading” of a woman’s 2023 complaint about Harry Benton “to see a very early pattern and practice of sexual harassment” by the now-disgraced ex-state representative, according to Springfield’s top watchdog.</p><p>But that didn’t stop Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch from supporting Benton’s reelection campaign in a purple suburban district to the tune of $1.4 million.</p><p>And it would take nearly three years for Welch to take any meaningful action to rein in Benton’s alleged misconduct — only after two other women reported similar complaints about the Plainfield Democrat, who resigned July 3 under a cloud of troubling claims.</p><p>That’s the takeaway from Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey’s long-awaited report released Friday, outlining the lewd comments Benton is accused of making to the first woman he hired in his district office, to the district director of a colleague and to the lobbyist whose complaint started his downfall earlier this year.</p><p>When McCuskey submitted his findings to Welch June 30, he ultimately recommended that the speaker stick with the initial steps Welch took after the most recent complaint in February: booting Benton from the House Democratic Caucus and stripping him of committee assignments and Speaker’s Office staff support.</p><p>McCuskey concluded Benton’s behavior violated the Illinois Human Rights Act against sexual harassment, but he advised against the House expulsion proceedings that Welch <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" >later threatened</a>, because they “would be lengthy and require a Special Session,” McCuskey wrote.</p><p>The inspector general didn’t evaluate Welch’s handling of the initial complaint, which fell outside the statute of limitations — and the latest complainant pushed back on what she deemed inaccuracies from her interview with McCuskey.</p><p>But the timeline laid out by McCuskey amplifies questions around how long Welch took to act, whether he could’ve prevented more misery — and whether he can hold onto his post in a chamber long mired in a culture of harassment.</p><p>“The Speaker must demonstrate a sincere desire to repair the harm he has done, and to correct the broken system in which we are all operating,” state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, said in a statement.</p><p>“[W]e have heard a series of excuses, victim blaming, and a failure to publicly acknowledge shortcomings. That has been disappointing,” said Cassidy, who voted “present” when Welch took the speaker’s gavel in 2021, citing concerns about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/28/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-michael-j-madigan-sexual-harassment-inquiry" target="_blank" ><u>unrelated past claims against Welch</u></a>.</p><p>She stopped short of calling for Welch to step down, as Hoffman Estates Democrat Fred Crespo and many Republicans have.</p><p>“Efforts to make changes to the laws and procedures around inappropriate behavior in the Capitol must center the experiences of victims,” Cassidy wrote. “Unless we examine these policies through the eyes and experiences of the people we’re intending to protect, we will continue to fall short.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, speaks during a 2024 news conference.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Welch issued a lengthy statement asserting his office “acted responsibly — following legal guidance, respecting the wishes of those who came forward, and taking decisive action as additional information established a pattern of misconduct.”</p><p>But the speaker also acknowledged a need “to strengthen our laws, improve our policies, modernize our practices, and continue building a General Assembly worthy of the trust placed in it by every employee, every legislator, and every Illinois resident we are privileged to serve.”</p><p>“My office will work with all members of the House to explore creating a centralized human resources office to assist all members as employers and support their district office employees, and we will bring in an outside expert to review this case and make additional recommendations,” Welch said in a statement. “We look forward to bringing together legislators, advocates, workplace experts, and other stakeholders to identify stronger protections, streamline reporting processes, improve support for those who come forward, and ensure greater clarity and accountability at every level.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Gov. JB Pritzker said the report makes “clear the General Assembly has more work to do. … The House now has a responsibility to resolve any unanswered questions, strengthen its harassment prevention and reporting procedures, and hold itself to the high standard the people of Illinois expect and deserve.”</p><p>Benton, who hasn’t given up his elected post as Wheatland Township highway commissioner, didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>He hasn’t addressed the scandal publicly, but Benton “denied ever saying or doing anything of a sexual nature” to the inspector general, and claimed never to have “attempted to sexually harass anyone,” McCuskey wrote.</p><h3>New Benton allegation</h3><p>Welch’s office received the first complaint just a few months after Benton was sworn into office, in an April 14, 2023, email from the new lawmaker's district office employee, detailing “many odd statements made to the employee as well as many statements of direct sexual harassment,” McCuskey wrote.</p><p>Benton allegedly told her the "reason I ran for office was to get away from my wife,” sent her a picture of an OnlyFans model and then asked her to send it back because it “[m]akes me feel better now I have this on you.”</p><p>Benton made other comments suggesting she would use office equipment to produce pornographic content for OnlyFans, and told her “I am keeping you off the pole with this job,” according to McCuskey.</p><p>When she told Benton she was going to a gun range with her boyfriend, Benton allegedly replied, "Wow, you're going to let him take you instead of me?”</p><p>“It doesn't take but a cursory reading of the April 14, 2023 E-mail documentation from the complaining district office employee to see a very early pattern and practice of sexual harassment by Rep. Harry Benton,” McCuskey wrote.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f70000" name="image-f70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/04f7f98/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7802878/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ba2504e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Former state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ba2504e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/749d0c7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ba2504e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F05%2F71%2F83c22d23485893449628b2f14ac5%2Fbenton.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But it wasn’t until after the employee resigned in June 2023 that Welch’s chief of staff and ethics officer “decided to confront Benton with these allegations,” McCuskey wrote, and they scheduled a Zoom meeting for July 20, 2023.</p><p>Benton invited the former employee to that meeting, which she did not attend.</p><p>“The reason I reported this was for the protection of the other women in the office,” she told Welch’s chief of staff, who encouraged her “to consider filing a report with the LIG.”</p><p>The complainant did not, and the Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House political committee went on to pump more than $1 million into Benton’s hotly contested reelection campaign.</p><p>In a statement, the former Benton staffer said, "My hope is that this experience, my experience, leads to something more important: honest reflection on the culture change, the policy change, and the personal change Springfield needs to attract and keep its brightest talent, and to make it a place where the work that matters is the focus.”</p><p>McCuskey didn’t delve into revelations from the Chicago Tribune that Welch himself later sent heart-eye emojis in social media interactions with the former staffer that made her uncomfortable, and used an encrypted messaging app to invite her to meet at a bar.</p><p>McCuskey’s report revealed a new allegation against Benton from another district director who said the representative “was creepy” with her at a Springfield bar following Latino Unity Day festivities in May 2025.</p><p>“Rep. Benton approached her and leaned over her and put his hand on her back,” McCuskey wrote, leaving her “very uncomfortable” until another person intervened.</p><p>McCuskey called it a prime example of unacceptable behavior as outlined in state-mandated training that Benton and other lawmakers receive yearly.</p><p>The latest alleged infraction happened in January at a bar in River North, where Benton told a lobbyist, “I might be a 5, but I f--- like a 10.”</p><h3>Complainant disputes parts of LIG report</h3><p>In a response from the lobbyist released Friday by the bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission along with McCuskey’s report, she disputed several points from McCuskey, who “did not record our one-on-one interview or take contemporaneous notes,” she wrote.</p><p>The woman reported that Benton said, “I am not hitting on you, unless you are interested,” and, “Let’s just say you are too hot to be a lobbyist.”</p><p>McCuskey’s report says she “immediately turned to” another male state representative nearby who replied, “What do you want me to do about it?”</p><p>In reality, according to the complainant, she called that lawmaker the next day, he “listened to my story, shared my concern and indicated … what Benton said to me was not an isolated incident.”</p><p>She also disputed a separate claim that McCuskey deemed unfounded: a complaint that Benton had photos on his phone of women in “various stages of undress which he claimed to be involved with romantically.”</p><p>“Every woman member of the General Assembly I interviewed said they had heard about the pictures on Benton's cell phone, but could not identify anyone who saw the pictures,” McCuskey wrote. But the lobbyist said she told McCuskey that Benton showed her such photos as well.</p><p>“While the errors in the report are concerning, the underlying facts remain the same,” she wrote.</p><p>Welch soon exiled Benton from their caucus in February, but Republicans said the report shows Benton should have been rooted out long before then.</p><p>“The time that passed from '23 to '26 is entirely too long for something to go unaddressed,” said state Rep. Jeff Keicher, the Sycamore Democrat who chairs the Ethics Commission that released the report.</p><p>“Had the initial reporting been treated in a different manner, we certainly could have interceded,” Keicher said. “There are others potentially involved here, if this was as widespread and [widely] known, that also had an obligation to step up and make reports.”</p><p>House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, has called for Welch to step down as speaker.</p><p>“The speaker continued to ignore it for three years [and] spent $1.4 million on a flawed member,” McCombie said. “The speaker let his ego, his ego not to lose one seat, come before values and principles of his caucus.</p><p>“He asks for respect and demands respect. He doesn't respect his own members. And he certainly doesn't respect the institution.”</p>
